questions.title: The working directory, staging area, and repository
questions.prompt: In Git, what's the difference between the working directory, the staging area (index), and the repository, and what do git add and git commit each actually do in terms of moving a change between them?
questions.modelAnswer: The working directory is the actual files on disk that you edit directly. The staging area (also called the index) is an intermediate holding area where you deliberately choose exactly which changes will go into the next commit -- it's a draft of the next commit, not the commit itself. The repository is the permanent, committed history -- a saved snapshot only exists there once a commit has actually been made. git add copies a change from the working directory into the staging area, marking it as 'included in the next commit' without creating any permanent record yet. git commit takes everything currently sitting in the staging area and permanently saves it as a new snapshot in the repository's history, along with a message describing it. This two-step design is deliberate: it lets you edit five files but choose to commit only two of them together as one logical change, leaving the other three staged or unstaged for a separate commit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as three stations a change passes through. I edit a file -- that's just sitting in my working directory, Git knows it changed but hasn't been told to care about it for the next commit yet. I run git add on it -- now it's staged, meaning I've deliberately said 'this specific change belongs in the next commit,' but nothing permanent has happened yet; I could still git reset it off the stage if I changed my mind. Only when I run git commit does Git actually take everything staged and lock it into the permanent history as a snapshot. The reason I bother with the staging step instead of committing everything at once is that it lets me build one clean, focused commit out of several files I touched, instead of one giant commit mixing unrelated changes together.
questions.example:
# edit file.py in the working directory

git add file.py        # stage the change (working dir -> staging area)
git commit -m 'Fix off-by-one in retry loop'  # staging area -> repository history
commonMistakes: Thinking git add permanently saves the change, when it only stages it for the next commit
Committing everything at once instead of staging related changes into one focused, logical commit
Forgetting an edited-but-unstaged file isn't included in the next git commit at all
Not realizing git status shows all three states (untracked/modified, staged, and clean) at once
keyPoints: Working directory = files on disk you edit; staging area = a draft of the next commit; repository = permanent committed history
git add moves a change from working directory to staging area
git commit moves everything staged into a permanent snapshot in the repository
Staging lets you build one focused commit out of a subset of your changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines the three areas
Correctly explains what add and commit each do
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Merge vs. rebase
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between git merge and git rebase when you want to bring your feature branch up to date with main? What does rebase actually do to your branch's commit history?
questions.modelAnswer: git merge creates a new commit -- a merge commit -- that has two parents, tying your branch's history and main's history together exactly as they both happened, side by side; the history ends up with a visible branch-and-merge shape. git rebase instead takes your branch's commits off their original base, replays main's new commits first, and then reapplies your commits one by one on top of that updated base -- as if you had started your branch from today's main all along. The practical result is a flat, linear history with no merge commit, which is easier to read later, but it rewrites your branch's commit history (new commit hashes), which is the critical reason you should never rebase a branch that other people have already pulled and are building on top of -- doing so breaks their copy's history.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the shape of the resulting history. If I merge main into my feature branch, I get a merge commit with two parents, and looking at the log later I can literally see where the two lines of work rejoined. If I rebase my feature branch onto main instead, Git detaches my commits, fast-forwards me to main's latest tip, and replays my commits on top one at a time -- the history ends up perfectly linear, like I'd built my branch starting from today's main the whole time. The tradeoff I always mention: rebase gives new commit hashes to every commit it replays, so if anyone else already has a copy of my branch and has built on top of it, rebasing out from under them breaks their history. My rule of thumb is rebase freely on a branch that's still only mine, and merge once it's shared.
questions.example:
# merge: keeps both histories, adds a merge commit
git checkout feature
git merge main

# rebase: replays feature's commits on top of main, linear history, new hashes
git checkout feature
git rebase main
commonMistakes: Rebasing a branch that others have already pulled and built on top of, breaking their history
Assuming rebase and merge produce the same resulting code with just different history shapes, without weighing the shared-branch risk
Not realizing rebase gives every replayed commit a brand-new hash
Force-pushing after a rebase without understanding why a normal push is rejected (the history diverged)
keyPoints: merge creates a two-parent merge commit, preserving both histories as they actually happened
rebase replays your commits on top of the updated base, producing a linear history
rebase rewrites commit hashes; never rebase a branch others have already pulled
Rule of thumb: rebase a private branch freely, merge once it's shared

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each command does to history
Correctly identifies the shared-branch rebase risk
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Regions vs. availability zones
questions.prompt: What's the difference between an Azure region and an availability zone, and why would a DBA care about deploying a database across multiple availability zones instead of just picking one?
questions.modelAnswer: A region is a geographic area containing one or more Azure datacenters, such as East US 2 or West Europe. An availability zone is a physically separate datacenter (or set of datacenters) within a region, each with its own independent power, cooling, and networking, so a failure in one zone -- a power outage, a cooling failure -- doesn't take down the others. A DBA cares because deploying a zone-redundant database spreads its replicas across different availability zones within the same region, protecting against a single datacenter-level failure without the added network latency of replicating all the way to a different, distant region. It's a middle ground between 'everything in one building' and full cross-region disaster recovery.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the distinction concrete: a region is the general area, like 'East US 2,' and an availability zone is one specific, physically separate building (or small cluster of buildings) inside that area with its own power and cooling. If I only deploy to one zone, a cooling failure or power outage in that one building can take my database down even though the region as a whole is fine. Spreading replicas across zones means that specific failure doesn't take me down, and because the zones are still close together in the same region, the latency cost of keeping replicas in sync is much lower than it would be replicating to an entirely different region on the other side of the country. I'd also flag that not every Azure region actually has availability zones, so this isn't something I can assume is available everywhere.
commonMistakes: Confusing a region (a geographic area) with an availability zone (a physically separate datacenter within that area)
Assuming every Azure region supports availability zones -- not all of them do
Assuming zone redundancy alone is sufficient disaster recovery for a regional outage, when that actually requires cross-region replication
Not connecting zone redundancy to the latency tradeoff versus cross-region replication
keyPoints: Region = a geographic area containing one or more datacenters
Availability zone = a physically separate datacenter within a region, with independent power/cooling/networking
Zone-redundant deployment protects against a single datacenter-level failure within a region
Zone redundancy alone is not disaster recovery for a full regional outage; not all regions have availability zones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes a region from an availability zone
Correctly explains why a DBA would use multiple zones
Notes the latency tradeoff vs. cross-region replication

questions.title: What a resource group actually is
questions.prompt: What is an Azure resource group, and what's the practical rule of thumb for deciding which resources belong in the same one?
questions.modelAnswer: A resource group is a logical container that holds related Azure resources for the purposes of management, access control, and billing -- it isn't a physical boundary, and resources inside it can even span different regions. Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it, which makes the grouping decision meaningful, not cosmetic. The practical rule of thumb is to group resources that share the same lifecycle -- things that should be deployed, updated, and eventually decommissioned together, like a single application's database, storage account, and app service -- rather than grouping purely by resource type or by team. Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time, regardless of which region it's deployed into.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as 'things that live and die together.' If I'm standing up one application's database, storage account, and web app, those all belong in the same resource group, because when that application is eventually retired, I want to delete all of it in one action instead of hunting down pieces scattered across different groups. The mistake I see most often is grouping by resource type instead -- 'all databases in one group, all storage in another' -- which sounds organized but actually makes it much easier to accidentally leave orphaned pieces behind when one application goes away, since nothing in that type-based group shares a lifecycle. The one hard rule I always remember is that a resource lives in exactly one resource group, no matter what region it's actually running in.
commonMistakes: Grouping resources by resource type (all databases together, all storage together) instead of by shared lifecycle
Forgetting that deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it
Putting a long-lived, shared resource into a short-lived project resource group where it could get accidentally deleted
Assuming a resource group is tied to a single region, rather than a logical grouping that can span regions
keyPoints: A resource group is a logical container for management, access control, and billing
Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it
Group resources by shared lifecycle (deployed/retired together), not by resource type
A resource belongs to exactly one resource group regardless of its region

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a resource group
Gives a usable rule of thumb for grouping resources
Mentions the delete-cascade consequence

questions.title: What the OSI/TCP-IP layers are actually for
questions.prompt: Why do networking models like TCP/IP split communication into separate layers (application, transport, network, link) instead of just treating 'sending data over the network' as one single step? Give a concrete example of why that separation matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Layering exists so each layer can solve one specific problem and depend on the layer below it without needing to know how that layer actually does its job -- the application layer just needs 'send these bytes to this address,' and doesn't need to know whether the data travels over Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or a cellular link underneath. The transport layer (TCP/UDP) is responsible for things like reliable delivery and ordering; the network layer (IP) is responsible for addressing and routing between networks; the link layer is responsible for actually moving frames across one physical hop. Because each layer only talks to the layer directly above and below it through a defined interface, a change at one layer -- switching from Wi-Fi to Ethernet, or a new routing protocol -- doesn't require every application on the internet to be rewritten. A concrete example: HTTPS traffic (application layer) works exactly the same way whether it travels over a home Wi-Fi link or a fiber connection at the office, because the link-layer details are invisible to it -- that's only possible because of the separation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with what breaks if you DIDN'T layer things: if 'sending data' were one single, monolithic step, then every time a new physical network technology came out -- 5G, a new Wi-Fi standard -- every application ever written would need to be updated to understand it. Layering means an application just hands data to TCP, TCP hands segments to IP, IP hands packets to the link layer, and each one only has to understand its own job and the interface to its neighbor. The example I'd give: I can browse the same HTTPS website whether I'm on my phone's cellular connection or my laptop's Ethernet cable, and the website's code never changes -- the link layer underneath is completely swapped out, and nothing above it even notices.
commonMistakes: Describing the layers as an arbitrary list to memorize rather than explaining why separation is useful
Not giving a concrete example of what the separation actually buys you
Confusing the order of the layers or what each one is actually responsible for
Assuming a change at one layer (like a new physical network type) requires changes at every other layer
keyPoints: Layering lets each layer solve one problem and depend on a defined interface to the layer below it
A layer doesn't need to know how the layer below it actually works internally
Changes at one layer (new physical network tech) don't require rewriting layers above it
Example: the same application-layer protocol works unchanged over completely different physical links

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of layering
Gives a concrete, accurate example
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What DNS actually resolves, and why caching matters
questions.prompt: In plain terms, what problem does DNS solve, and why does a DNS record's TTL (time to live) matter if you need to change where a domain points?
questions.modelAnswer: Computers route traffic using IP addresses, not names, but IP addresses are hard for people to remember and can change over time -- DNS solves that by acting as a lookup system that translates a human-readable domain name (like example.com) into the IP address a computer actually needs to connect to. TTL is the number of seconds a DNS record is allowed to be cached by resolvers and other machines along the way before they're required to look it up again -- a long TTL (say, 24 hours) reduces repeated lookup traffic and speeds up resolution for everyone, but it also means that if you change the IP address a domain points to, machines that already cached the old record won't see the change until their cached copy expires. That's why, before a planned server migration or IP change, it's standard practice to lower a record's TTL well in advance, so the eventual cutover propagates quickly instead of leaving some users hitting the old IP for up to a full day.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame DNS as the internet's phone book -- it turns a name a person can remember into the actual IP address a connection needs. The part that trips people up in practice is TTL: if a record's TTL is set to 24 hours and I change the IP today, anyone whose resolver already cached the old answer won't see my new IP until that cached entry expires, possibly a full day later. So if I know I'm migrating a server next week, my first move now is lowering that record's TTL to something short, like 5 minutes, and waiting for the old long TTL to fully expire everywhere first -- only then do I actually make the IP change, so the cutover is fast and I'm not stuck half-migrated with some users still landing on the old server for a day.
commonMistakes: Describing DNS only as 'translating names to numbers' without explaining why that's actually needed
Not understanding that TTL controls how long a cached answer is considered valid before being re-looked-up
Changing a DNS record's IP without first lowering its TTL in advance of a planned migration
Assuming a DNS change takes effect everywhere instantly, ignoring caching entirely
keyPoints: DNS translates human-readable domain names into the IP addresses computers actually connect to
TTL controls how long a DNS answer can be cached before it must be looked up again
A long TTL means a changed record can take that long to be seen everywhere
Lower a record's TTL in advance of a planned IP change so the cutover propagates quickly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what problem DNS solves
Correctly explains TTL and its practical consequence
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Reading Linux permissions and chmod's numeric notation
questions.prompt: Looking at the output -rwxr-xr-- for a file, what does each character and group of characters mean, and what numeric chmod command would produce that exact permission set?
questions.modelAnswer: The first character (-) indicates the file type -- a dash means a regular file (a d would mean a directory). The next nine characters break into three groups of three: owner (rwx), group (r-x), and others (r--), each representing read, write, and execute permission in that order, with a dash meaning that permission is absent. Here, the owner can read, write, and execute; the group can read and execute but not write; others can only read. Numeric (octal) notation represents each group as a sum: read=4, write=2, execute=1. Owner rwx = 4+2+1 = 7; group r-x = 4+0+1 = 5; others r-- = 4+0+0 = 4. So chmod 754 <filename> produces exactly that permission set.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd read it left to right: the leading dash tells me it's a regular file, not a directory. Then I split the remaining nine characters into three chunks of three -- owner, group, others -- and read each chunk as read/write/execute in that fixed order, with a dash meaning 'no, this is not granted.' So rwx for the owner, r-x for the group, r-- for others. To turn that into a chmod number, I add up read(4)+write(2)+execute(1) per chunk: owner is 7, group is 5, others is 4, giving chmod 754. I always double check the order is owner-group-others, since getting that backwards is the single most common mistake I see with permissions.
questions.example:
-rwxr-xr--  1 alice  devs  1024 Jan 5 10:00 deploy.sh

# owner (alice): rwx = 4+2+1 = 7
# group (devs):  r-x = 4+0+1 = 5
# others:        r-- = 4+0+0 = 4

chmod 754 deploy.sh
commonMistakes: Mixing up the order of owner/group/others when reading the permission string
Forgetting the leading character indicates file type, not a permission
Adding the numeric values incorrectly (e.g. treating write as 1 instead of 2)
Confusing chmod's numeric (octal) mode with its symbolic mode (u+x, g-w, etc.) and mixing syntax between them
keyPoints: The leading character is file type; the remaining nine split into owner/group/others, each read-write-execute
A dash in any position means that permission is not granted
Numeric mode sums read=4, write=2, execute=1 per group
chmod 754 sets owner=rwx, group=r-x, others=r--

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads the permission string character by character
Correctly converts to the matching numeric chmod value
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What sudo actually does, and why not just use root
questions.prompt: What does running a command with sudo actually do, and why is it generally considered better practice than just logging in as the root user and staying there?
questions.modelAnswer: sudo (superuser do) lets an authorized user run a specific command with elevated (typically root) privileges for just that one command, after authenticating with their own password -- the user's own identity is preserved and logged, rather than becoming an anonymous 'root' with no record of who actually did what. Staying logged in as root the whole time removes that accountability: every action taken is attributed only to 'root,' not to the specific person who ran it, which makes auditing a mistake or an intrusion far harder after the fact. sudo also lets an administrator grant narrowly scoped privilege -- a specific user can be permitted to run only certain commands as root via the sudoers file, rather than an all-or-nothing choice between a normal user and full root access. The practical safety benefit is reducing the blast radius of a mistake too: a single mistyped destructive command run under sudo still requires deliberately invoking sudo for that one command, rather than every single command in an entire session already running with root's full, unrestricted power.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain sudo as 'borrow root's power for one command, with your own name still attached to the receipt.' Every sudo invocation gets logged with the actual username that ran it, which means if something goes wrong at 2 AM, there's a real audit trail of who did what, not just an anonymous 'root did this.' Staying logged in as root the entire time throws that away -- and it also means every single command in that session, including a typo, runs with full unrestricted power, whereas with sudo at least each dangerous command requires a deliberate extra step to invoke. The other practical benefit is that sudo lets me grant a junior teammate permission to run exactly the specific commands they need as root, through the sudoers file, without ever handing them the actual root password or blanket access to everything.
commonMistakes: Thinking sudo and root are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
Not knowing sudo preserves an audit trail of which actual user ran a privileged command
Assuming sudo access is all-or-nothing rather than something that can be scoped to specific commands via sudoers
Staying in a root shell for convenience instead of using sudo per command, increasing the blast radius of any mistake
keyPoints: sudo elevates privilege for one command at a time, under the user's own authenticated identity
sudo actions are logged against the real user, unlike anonymous actions taken as root
sudoers can scope exactly which commands a given user is allowed to run with elevated privilege
Staying logged in as root removes accountability and increases the blast radius of any single mistake

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what sudo actually does
Correctly explains the accountability/audit-trail benefit over staying as root
Mentions scoped privilege via sudoers

questions.title: What a shebang line actually does
questions.prompt: What does the first line of a script like #!/bin/bash or #!/usr/bin/env python3 actually do, and what happens if a script is missing it or has the wrong one?
questions.modelAnswer: The shebang (#!) line tells the operating system which interpreter should be used to execute the rest of the file when the script is run directly as a program (for example, ./script.sh) -- the kernel reads that first line and launches the specified interpreter, handing it the rest of the file to run, rather than trying to execute the file's contents as raw machine code. #!/bin/bash hard-codes the absolute path to bash; #!/usr/bin/env python3 instead asks the env command to find whichever python3 is first on the current PATH, which is more portable across machines where python3 might live in a different location. If a script is missing a shebang entirely, running it directly may fail or get interpreted by whatever shell happens to invoke it (which is unreliable) -- though it can still be run explicitly with bash script.sh, bypassing the shebang. If the shebang names the wrong interpreter (pointing a Python script at bash, for example), the script will fail immediately with syntax errors, since bash doesn't understand Python syntax at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the shebang line as a note left for the kernel: 'don't try to run this file yourself, hand it to this interpreter instead.' If I write #!/bin/bash at the top of a script and run it with ./deploy.sh, the kernel sees that line, launches /bin/bash, and feeds it the rest of the file. For Python specifically I almost always use #!/usr/bin/env python3 instead of hard-coding a path like /usr/bin/python3, because env looks up whatever python3 is first on PATH, which means the script still works correctly on a machine where Python lives somewhere slightly different, like inside a virtual environment. If I forget the shebang entirely, ./script.sh might fail outright or get picked up by whatever the default shell happens to be, which is exactly the kind of inconsistency I don't want -- so I treat it as non-negotiable on the first line of every script I write.
questions.example:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print('hello')

# chmod +x greet.py && ./greet.py
# -> kernel reads the shebang, launches python3, hands it the rest of the file
commonMistakes: Omitting the shebang line and assuming the script will always be run by the 'right' interpreter by default
Hard-coding an interpreter's absolute path when a more portable #!/usr/bin/env <name> would work across more machines
Forgetting the script also needs execute permission (chmod +x) for the shebang to matter when run directly
Assuming the shebang line is just a comment with no real effect, rather than an instruction read by the kernel
keyPoints: The shebang line tells the kernel which interpreter to use to run the rest of the file
#!/usr/bin/env <interpreter> finds the interpreter via PATH, which is more portable than a hard-coded absolute path
A missing or wrong shebang can cause the script to fail or be run by the wrong interpreter
A script also needs execute permission (chmod +x) for direct execution with the shebang to take effect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the shebang line does
Correctly explains the env-based pattern's portability benefit
Correctly explains the consequence of a missing/wrong shebang

questions.title: Images vs. containers: what's the actual difference
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a Docker image and a Docker container? If you run docker run three times from the same image, what do you end up with?
questions.modelAnswer: A Docker image is a read-only, packaged template -- the application's code, its dependencies, and the filesystem it needs, bundled together along with instructions for how to start it -- that doesn't change once built. A container is a running (or stopped) instance created from an image, with its own writable layer stacked on top of the image's read-only layers, its own process, and its own isolated view of the filesystem and network. The relationship is like a class and an object, or a recipe and a cooked dish: the image is the fixed template, and a container is one live instance made from it. Running docker run three times from the same image produces three completely separate, independent containers -- each gets its own writable layer and its own running process, and a change made inside one container (writing a file, for instance) has no effect on the other two or on the original image itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use the recipe-and-dish analogy: the image is the recipe, fixed and unchanging once written down. Every time I run docker run against that image, I bake a brand-new dish -- a container -- and each one is completely independent of the others, even though they all started from the identical recipe. If I run docker run nginx three times, I get three separate running nginx containers, each with its own writable layer on top of the shared read-only image layers; writing a file inside container #1 doesn't appear in container #2 or #3, and definitely doesn't modify the nginx image itself. That immutability of the image is actually the whole point -- I can delete all three containers, run docker run nginx again, and get a fresh, totally clean instance identical to how the first one started, because the image itself was never touched.
commonMistakes: Using 'image' and 'container' interchangeably as if they're the same thing
Assuming running an image multiple times modifies the original image itself
Not realizing each container gets its own independent writable layer, isolated from other containers made from the same image
Assuming a change made inside one running container is visible to other containers started from the same image
keyPoints: An image is a read-only, fixed template; a container is a running (or stopped) instance created from it
Each container has its own writable layer and its own isolated process/filesystem view
Running the same image multiple times produces multiple independent containers, not shared state
The image itself never changes no matter how many containers are created from it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes an image from a container
Correctly explains the outcome of running the same image multiple times
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Create a branch, commit, and push it
questions.prompt: Write the sequence of Git commands to create a new branch called feature/retry-logic off of main, switch to it, stage and commit a change with the message 'Add retry logic for API calls', and push that branch to the remote for the first time.
questions.code: # Starting point: on main, with a local modified file
questions.modelAnswer: git checkout -b feature/retry-logic creates the new branch and switches to it in one step (equivalent to git branch feature/retry-logic followed by git checkout feature/retry-logic). git add <file> (or git add . for everything changed) stages the change, and git commit -m '...' commits it. The first push of a brand-new local branch needs -u (or --set-upstream) -- git push -u origin feature/retry-logic -- which both pushes the branch and records the link between this local branch and its remote counterpart, so every subsequent git push or git pull on this branch works without needing to repeat the remote and branch name.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run git checkout -b feature/retry-logic to branch off main and land directly on the new branch, then git add . and git commit -m 'Add retry logic for API calls' to capture the change. For the push, I always remember the first push of a new branch needs the -u flag -- git push -u origin feature/retry-logic -- because without it, Git doesn't know this local branch should track that remote branch, and I'd get an error or have to type the full remote/branch combination every time afterward. Once that first -u push is done, every later push or pull on this branch is just a plain git push or git pull.
questions.example:
git checkout -b feature/retry-logic
git add .
git commit -m 'Add retry logic for API calls'
git push -u origin feature/retry-logic
commonMistakes: Forgetting -u on the first push, then being confused by the 'no upstream branch' error on a later plain git push
Running git branch feature/retry-logic without also switching to it via checkout or switch
Committing with no staged changes (forgetting git add) and getting 'nothing to commit'
Writing a vague commit message instead of describing what the change actually does
keyPoints: git checkout -b <name> creates and switches to a new branch in one step
git add stages changes; git commit -m saves them with a message
The first push of a new branch needs -u (--set-upstream) to link it to the remote
After the first -u push, plain git push/pull work without repeating the remote/branch name

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct branch creation and switch command
Correct add/commit sequence
Correct first-push syntax including -u

questions.title: Resolve a merge conflict
questions.prompt: You run git merge main into your feature branch and Git reports a conflict in config.py. Walk through, with the actual conflict markers, how you'd read the conflict and the commands you'd run to resolve it and complete the merge.
questions.code:
# After: git merge main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
questions.modelAnswer: Git marks the conflicting section of the file directly with conflict markers: everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your current branch's version, and everything between ======= and >>>>>>> main is the incoming branch's version. Resolving it means opening the file, deciding what the final content should actually be -- keeping one side, the other, or a combination -- and then deleting all three marker lines, leaving only the correct final code behind. After editing the file, git add config.py marks it as resolved, and git commit (with no -m needed, since Git pre-fills a merge commit message) completes the merge.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I open config.py and see the HEAD section showing TIMEOUT = 30 and the main section showing TIMEOUT = 60, I read that as: my branch has 30, main has 60, and Git genuinely doesn't know which one I want, so it's leaving both in and asking me. I'd decide the actual correct value -- say main's 60 is right because it was a deliberate recent fix -- delete all three marker lines and the version I'm not keeping, leaving just TIMEOUT = 60. Then git add config.py to tell Git this file's conflict is resolved, and git commit to finish the merge, which Git already pre-fills with a sensible merge commit message I can usually accept as-is.
questions.example:
<<<<<<< HEAD
TIMEOUT = 30
=======
TIMEOUT = 60
>>>>>>> main

# After resolving (decided main's value is correct):
TIMEOUT = 60

# Then:
git add config.py
git commit
commonMistakes: Leaving one or more of the conflict marker lines in the file by accident
Not running git add on the resolved file before committing, leaving the merge incomplete
Picking a side without actually reading what each version does, instead of deciding the genuinely correct final content
Panicking and running git merge --abort unnecessarily for a conflict that just needed a straightforward manual resolution
keyPoints: <<<<<<< HEAD marks the start of your current branch's version; ======= separates it from the incoming version; >>>>>>> marks the end
Resolving means deciding the final content and removing all marker lines
git add marks the file as resolved; git commit completes the merge
git merge --abort is available to back out entirely if needed, but isn't required for a normal conflict

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads and explains the conflict markers
Correctly resolves to valid final content
Correct add/commit sequence to complete the merge

questions.title: Write a .gitignore for a Python AI project
questions.prompt: Write a .gitignore file for a Python project that uses a virtual environment, has a .env file holding API keys, and generates __pycache__ directories, making sure none of those ever get committed.
questions.modelAnswer: .gitignore tells Git which files and directories to never track or stage, even with git add . -- each line is a pattern matched against file and directory names anywhere in the repo (unless anchored with a leading slash). A virtual environment directory (commonly venv/ or .venv/) should always be ignored, since it's large, machine-specific, and fully reproducible from requirements.txt -- committing it bloats the repo for no benefit. .env should be ignored because it holds real secrets (API keys), and a secret committed to Git history is extremely difficult to fully remove later even after deleting the file -- the safe move is never letting it be committed in the first place. __pycache__/ (and *.pyc) should be ignored because it's regenerated automatically by Python and carries no real content worth tracking.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write a .gitignore with venv/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, and .env as the core lines for this project. The one I'm most careful about is .env -- I always add it to .gitignore before I ever create the file with real keys in it, not after, because once a secret has been committed, it's sitting in Git history forever, even if I delete the file in a later commit, and the only real fix at that point is rotating the leaked key, not just deleting the file. I'd also make sure a project ships a .env.example with placeholder values committed instead, so teammates know what variables they need to set without the real secret ever touching the repo.
commonMistakes: Adding .env to .gitignore only after it's already been committed once, leaving the secret in Git history
Forgetting __pycache__/ and *.pyc, letting auto-generated files clutter every commit
Committing the venv/ directory, bloating the repo with large, machine-specific, reproducible files
Not providing a .env.example with placeholder values so teammates know what variables are needed
keyPoints: .gitignore prevents matched files/directories from ever being tracked, even with git add .
Virtual environment directories should be ignored -- large, reproducible, machine-specific
.env (real secrets) must never be committed; add it to .gitignore before creating the file
Auto-generated files like __pycache__/ and *.pyc should always be ignored

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct .gitignore patterns for all three cases
Correctly explains the risk of committing .env/secrets
Mentions .env.example as a teammate-friendly practice

questions.title: Diagnosing a connectivity problem with ping, traceroute, and curl
questions.code: # You can't reach https://api.example.com from your machine
questions.prompt: Write the sequence of commands you'd run, in order, to narrow down why https://api.example.com is unreachable from your machine -- checking basic connectivity, the network path, and the actual HTTP response.
questions.modelAnswer: The logical order goes from the most basic layer up to the actual application response, so each step rules out a category of problem before moving to the next. First, ping api.example.com checks basic reachability and whether the hostname resolves at all -- if it fails to resolve, that's a DNS problem before anything else. Next, traceroute api.example.com (or tracert on Windows) shows the path packets take and where they stop responding, which narrows down whether the failure is on the local network, somewhere in the middle of the internet, or at the destination itself. Finally, curl -v https://api.example.com shows the actual HTTP-level response (or exactly where the connection attempt failed, such as a TLS handshake failure or an HTTP error code), which is the most informative step once basic network reachability has been confirmed -- it's the step that tells you if the problem is actually at the network layer at all, or if it's an application-level issue like an expired certificate or a 403 response.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work from the bottom up: ping api.example.com first, mainly to confirm the name even resolves to an IP and that basic packets get a reply -- if this fails with 'unknown host,' I already know it's DNS, not the application. Next I'd run traceroute api.example.com to see how far the packets actually get before something stops responding; if it dies at my own router, that's a local network issue, if it dies somewhere out on the internet, that's not something I can fix from my end. Only once I'm confident basic connectivity works would I reach for curl -v https://api.example.com, because that's the step that actually shows me the HTTP-level detail -- the TLS handshake, the response headers, the status code -- which is usually where the real answer is if ping and traceroute both looked fine.
questions.example:
ping api.example.com
traceroute api.example.com   # tracert api.example.com on Windows
curl -v https://api.example.com
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to curl without first confirming basic reachability and DNS resolution
Not recognizing traceroute as the step that narrows down WHERE along the path the failure occurs
Assuming a failed ping always means the server is down, without considering the server may simply block ICMP
Not using curl -v (verbose) and missing the actual TLS/HTTP-level detail that explains the real failure
keyPoints: ping first checks basic reachability and DNS resolution
traceroute narrows down where along the network path the failure occurs
curl -v reveals the actual HTTP/TLS-level response or failure point
Work from the most basic layer up to the application layer, ruling out categories in order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, logically ordered sequence of commands
Correctly explains what each command rules in/out
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Fix a permission and ownership problem
questions.code:
# deploy.sh is owned by root:root with mode 644, and the 'deploy' user needs to
# own it and be able to execute it, without giving execute permission to everyone
questions.prompt: Write the commands to change deploy.sh's owner to the deploy user (keeping its group as deploy), and set its permissions so the owner can read/write/execute, the group can read/execute, and others have no access at all.
questions.modelAnswer: chown changes ownership; the owner:group form lets both be set in one command: chown deploy:deploy deploy.sh. For the permissions, the target is owner=rwx (7), group=r-x (5), others=--- (0), which as a single chmod numeric value is 750: chmod 750 deploy.sh. Running chown before chmod isn't strictly required order-wise, but it's a sensible habit since getting ownership right first means the permission bits are being set for the actual intended owner, not root.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run chown deploy:deploy deploy.sh first to make sure both the owner and group are what I actually want. Then chmod 750 deploy.sh -- owner gets 7 (rwx), group gets 5 (r-x), and others get 0, meaning no read, write, or execute access at all for anyone outside the owner and group. I specifically wouldn't use 755 here, since that would let literally anyone on the system execute and read the script, and the requirement was explicitly 'no access for others.'
questions.example:
chown deploy:deploy deploy.sh
chmod 750 deploy.sh

# verify:
ls -l deploy.sh
# -rwxr-x---  1 deploy  deploy  ... deploy.sh
commonMistakes: Using chmod 755 instead of 750, accidentally granting read/execute access to 'others'
Changing permissions before ownership, or forgetting to change the group along with the owner
Confusing chown's user:group syntax and only changing the owner, leaving the group unchanged by mistake
Not verifying the final result with ls -l after making the changes
keyPoints: chown user:group sets both owner and group in one command
chmod 750 gives owner rwx, group r-x, others no access at all
Others=0 explicitly means no read, write, or execute for anyone outside owner/group
Always verify the result with ls -l after changing ownership or permissions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct chown command and syntax
Correct chmod numeric value for the exact required permissions
Mentions verifying the result

questions.title: Find and clean up old log files
questions.code:
# /var/log/app/ contains many .log files; delete any that haven't been
# modified in the last 30 days, without deleting anything else in that directory
questions.prompt: Write a single find command that locates .log files under /var/log/app/ older than 30 days and deletes them.
questions.modelAnswer: find /var/log/app/ -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete combines all the needed filters: -type f restricts to regular files (not directories), -name '*.log' restricts to files ending in .log, -mtime +30 restricts to files whose content was last modified more than 30 days ago, and -delete removes every file that matched all three prior conditions. It's good practice to first run the exact same command without -delete (or with -print) to see the list of files that would be deleted, confirming it's the expected set, before actually running the destructive version.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write find /var/log/app/ -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete. Before I ever add -delete, though, I always run the identical command without it first -- just find /var/log/app/ -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -- and actually read through the list of files it prints, to make sure I'm not about to delete something I didn't mean to, like a log that was touched by a process recently even though it's logically 'old.' Only once that dry-run list looks right do I add -delete and re-run it for real. I'd also point out -mtime +30 means strictly more than 30 full days, not '30 days or older' in a loose sense, which matters if someone expects an exact boundary.
questions.example:
# dry run first:
find /var/log/app/ -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30

# then actually delete:
find /var/log/app/ -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete
commonMistakes: Running -delete directly without first dry-running the find command to see what would be matched
Forgetting -type f, which could also match a directory named something.log
Using -mtime +30 and assuming it means exactly 30 days rather than more than 30 full days
Piping find's output to rm via xargs when -delete already does the job more safely and directly
keyPoints: find combines -type, -name, and -mtime filters, with -delete acting on everything that matches all of them
-type f restricts matches to regular files, avoiding accidentally matching directories
-mtime +30 means more than 30 full days since last modification
Always dry-run a destructive find command (without -delete) before actually deleting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct find command with all required filters and -delete
Mentions dry-running before deleting
Correctly explains -mtime's meaning

questions.title: Write a Bash loop with a conditional
questions.code:
# servers.txt contains one hostname per line.
# For each one, ping it once; print 'UP' or 'DOWN'.
questions.prompt: Write a Bash script that reads servers.txt line by line, pings each hostname once, and prints '<hostname>: UP' or '<hostname>: DOWN' depending on whether the ping succeeded.
questions.modelAnswer: A while read loop is the standard, safe way to process a file line by line in Bash, since a for loop over $(cat file) would incorrectly split on whitespace within a line rather than just on newlines. ping -c 1 sends exactly one ping instead of the default continuous stream, and redirecting its output to /dev/null suppresses the ping output itself since only the result is needed. The if statement checks ping's exit status directly ($? via the if ping ...; then shorthand) -- an exit status of 0 means success (UP), any non-zero exit status means failure (DOWN).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write: while read -r host; do if ping -c 1 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "$host: UP"; else echo "$host: DOWN"; fi; done < servers.txt. I use while read -r specifically instead of looping over $(cat servers.txt), because the latter would split on any whitespace inside a line, not just between lines, which can silently break on unexpected input. -c 1 limits ping to a single attempt so the script doesn't hang waiting on a continuous ping stream, and redirecting both stdout and stderr to /dev/null keeps the script's own UP/DOWN output clean. The if ping ...; then pattern directly uses ping's exit code -- 0 for success, non-zero for failure -- without needing to capture it into a separate variable first.
questions.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while read -r host; do
  if ping -c 1 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "$host: UP"
  else
    echo "$host: DOWN"
  fi
done < servers.txt
commonMistakes: Using for host in $(cat servers.txt) instead of while read -r, risking incorrect word-splitting
Forgetting -c 1 on ping, causing the script to hang on a continuous ping stream
Not redirecting ping's own output to /dev/null, cluttering the script's actual UP/DOWN output
Not quoting "$host", which can break on a hostname containing unexpected characters
keyPoints: while read -r line safely processes a file line by line in Bash
ping -c 1 limits to a single ping attempt instead of a continuous stream
if command; then ... uses the command's exit status directly (0 = success)
Quote variables like "$host" to avoid word-splitting issues

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct while read loop reading the file line by line
Correct ping usage and exit-status check
Correct quoting and output suppression

questions.title: Read a JSON config file in Python
questions.prompt: Write a Python script that reads config.json, loads it into a dictionary, and prints the hostname and port in the format 'Connecting to db01:5432'. Handle the case where the file doesn't exist by printing a clear error instead of crashing with a traceback.
questions.modelAnswer: json.load(file_object) parses an already-open file's JSON content directly into a Python dictionary (as opposed to json.loads, which parses a JSON string that's already in memory). Opening the file inside a with statement ensures it's properly closed even if something goes wrong while reading it. Wrapping the open() call in a try/except FileNotFoundError catches specifically the case where config.json doesn't exist, letting the script print a clear, intentional error message instead of letting an unhandled traceback reach the user. Accessing config['hostname'] and config['port'] pulls the needed values out of the parsed dictionary by key.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write: try: with open('config.json') as f: config = json.load(f) and then print(f"Connecting to {config['hostname']}:{config['port']}") inside the try block, with except FileNotFoundError: print('config.json not found') as the fallback. I always open a file inside a with block rather than calling open() and close() manually, since with guarantees the file handle is released even if json.load() itself throws partway through. I'm specific about catching FileNotFoundError rather than a bare except, because a bare except would also silently swallow a genuine JSON syntax error in the file, which I'd want to see as its own distinct problem, not hidden behind the same generic error message.
questions.example:
import json

try:
    with open('config.json') as f:
        config = json.load(f)
    print(f"Connecting to {config['hostname']}:{config['port']}")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print('Error: config.json not found')
commonMistakes: Using json.loads() on a file object instead of json.load(), or vice versa on a string
Not using a with block, risking the file handle staying open if an error occurs while reading
Catching a bare except instead of FileNotFoundError specifically, hiding other real errors like invalid JSON
Accessing a dictionary key directly with [] when it might be missing, instead of handling that case too
keyPoints: json.load(file) parses an open file's JSON content into a dict; json.loads(string) parses a string
Use a with block when opening a file so it's always properly closed
Catch FileNotFoundError specifically, not a bare except, to avoid hiding unrelated errors
Access parsed values by key once the dict is loaded

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct JSON loading and file handling with a with block
Correct, specific FileNotFoundError handling
Correct output formatting

questions.title: Run a shell command from Python and capture its output
questions.code: # Run `df -h /` and capture its output as text in Python, raising an error if the command fails
questions.prompt: Write a Python snippet using the subprocess module that runs df -h / , captures its standard output as a string, and raises an exception automatically if the command exits with a non-zero status.
questions.modelAnswer: subprocess.run() is the modern, recommended way to run an external command from Python. Passing the command as a list of strings (['df', '-h', '/']) rather than one combined string avoids shell-injection risk and ambiguity about how arguments are split. capture_output=True captures both stdout and stderr; text=True decodes that captured output as a string instead of raw bytes. check=True makes subprocess.run() automatically raise a CalledProcessError if the command's exit status is non-zero, instead of silently returning a result object the caller has to remember to inspect. The captured text is available afterward as result.stdout.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write: result = subprocess.run(['df', '-h', '/'], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True) and then use result.stdout for the captured output. I always pass the command as a list of separate arguments rather than a single string with shell=True, since the list form avoids shell-injection risk entirely and doesn't depend on exactly how a string would get split into arguments. check=True is the detail I never skip for a command whose failure actually matters -- without it, a failed df command just returns silently with a non-zero result.returncode that's easy to forget to check, whereas check=True raises immediately and loudly if something goes wrong.
questions.example:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ['df', '-h', '/'],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    check=True,
)
print(result.stdout)
commonMistakes: Passing the command as a single string with shell=True instead of a list, introducing shell-injection risk
Forgetting check=True, then not noticing when the command actually failed
Forgetting text=True and getting raw bytes back instead of a usable string
Using the older, less safe os.system() or os.popen() instead of subprocess.run()
keyPoints: subprocess.run() with a list of arguments is the safe, modern way to run an external command
capture_output=True plus text=True captures stdout/stderr as a decoded string
check=True raises CalledProcessError automatically on a non-zero exit status
Avoid shell=True with a raw string unless there's a specific reason to need shell features

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct subprocess.run() call with the command as a list
Correctly captures output as text
Correctly uses check=True for automatic failure handling

questions.title: Write a basic Dockerfile for a small Python script
questions.code: # app.py (a small script) and requirements.txt sit in the project root
questions.prompt: Write a Dockerfile that builds an image for a small Python application: it should use a slim official Python base image, copy requirements.txt in and install dependencies, then copy the rest of the application code in, and run app.py when the container starts.
questions.modelAnswer: FROM python:3.12-slim selects a lightweight official Python base image rather than the full image, which keeps the final image smaller. WORKDIR /app sets the working directory inside the image so subsequent commands operate relative to it. Copying requirements.txt in and running pip install before copying the rest of the application code is a deliberate ordering choice: Docker caches each instruction's layer, so as long as requirements.txt hasn't changed, Docker can reuse the cached dependency-install layer on a rebuild even if the application code changed, making rebuilds much faster. COPY . . then copies the remaining application files in. CMD ["python", "app.py"] defines the default command the container runs when started, using the exec form (a JSON array) rather than a plain string, which runs the process directly instead of through an extra shell layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write FROM python:3.12-slim, then WORKDIR /app, then COPY requirements.txt . followed by RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt, then COPY . . , then CMD ["python", "app.py"]. The reason I copy requirements.txt and install dependencies BEFORE copying the rest of the code, rather than just doing COPY . . once at the top, is Docker's layer caching: if I only ever change app.py and never touch requirements.txt, this ordering means the pip install layer gets reused from cache on every rebuild instead of re-running every single time, which can save a real amount of build time. I use the --no-cache-dir flag on pip to avoid bloating the image with pip's own download cache, which serves no purpose inside a container that gets rebuilt from scratch each time anyway.
questions.example:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
commonMistakes: Copying all the application code in before installing dependencies, breaking Docker's layer caching on every rebuild
Using the full python image instead of the slim variant, producing an unnecessarily large image
Writing CMD as a plain string (CMD python app.py) instead of the exec-form JSON array
Forgetting to set WORKDIR, leaving files scattered relative to the image's default root directory
keyPoints: Copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying the rest of the code, to benefit from layer caching
A slim base image keeps the final image smaller than the full image
CMD should use the exec-form JSON array, not a plain shell string
WORKDIR sets a consistent working directory inside the image for subsequent instructions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Dockerfile structure and instruction order
Correctly explains the layer-caching reason for that order
Correct CMD syntax (exec form)

questions.title: Recovering from a detached HEAD state
questions.prompt: You run git checkout on an old commit hash to look at some old code, make a couple of commits while exploring, and then realize Git has been warning you about a 'detached HEAD' the whole time. What does that actually mean, and how do you recover your new commits without losing them?
questions.modelAnswer: Normally HEAD points at a branch name, and a branch name moves forward automatically with each new commit. Checking out a specific commit hash instead of a branch name puts HEAD directly on that commit -- detached from any branch -- so any new commits made in that state still get created, but nothing is tracking or advancing a branch pointer to include them; they exist, but they're not reachable from any branch. The real risk is that if you simply check out a branch again without first doing something about those commits, they become effectively orphaned, unreachable from any branch name, and eventually eligible for Git's garbage collection. The fix is to create a new branch right at the detached commit before switching away: git branch new-branch-name (or git switch -c new-branch-name), which gives those otherwise-orphaned commits a real branch name pointing at them, making them permanently reachable again.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I notice the detached HEAD warning, before I do anything else, I'd run git branch recovered-work right where I am -- that creates a brand-new branch pointing at exactly the commit I'm currently sitting on, including whatever I've committed since detaching. That one command is the entire fix: it takes commits that were about to become unreachable the moment I switched to another branch, and gives them a permanent home. I'd specifically avoid just checking out main first and trying to figure it out after, because at that point the commits are still technically findable with git reflog for a while, but it's a much more stressful recovery than just branching from where I already am before switching away.
questions.example:
# Oops -- already on a detached HEAD after a couple commits
git branch recovered-work   # points a new branch at the current (detached) commit
git checkout recovered-work # now safely on a real branch with those commits

# If you already switched away: git reflog can help locate the orphaned commit hash
commonMistakes: Switching to another branch before creating a new branch to capture the detached commits, risking orphaning them
Panicking and assuming the commits are permanently lost rather than recoverable via git branch or git reflog
Not understanding that new commits CAN be made in a detached HEAD state -- they just aren't tracked by any branch
Confusing a detached HEAD with an actual error; Git allows it deliberately for inspecting old history
keyPoints: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly at a commit, not at a branch name
Commits made in a detached HEAD state exist but aren't reachable from any branch
Create a new branch at the current commit (git branch <name>) before switching away, to keep the commits reachable
git reflog is a fallback to recover an already-orphaned commit hash if you switched away too soon

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what detached HEAD means
Correctly explains the risk of losing the commits
Provides the correct recovery fix (branch at the current commit)

questions.title: You just committed an API key
questions.prompt: You accidentally commit a file containing a real AI provider API key and push it to a shared GitHub repository. You catch it a few minutes later. What do you actually need to do, in order, and why isn't simply deleting the file in a new commit enough?
questions.modelAnswer: Deleting the file in a new commit only removes it from the current, latest snapshot of the repository -- the commit that actually added the key is still sitting in the repository's history, fully intact and retrievable by anyone with access to the repo (or anyone who already pulled or cloned it before the fix), so the key is still fully exposed even after the 'fix' commit. The first and most urgent action, before anything about Git itself, is rotating the key -- going to the provider's dashboard and revoking the leaked key, generating a new one -- because once a secret has been pushed anywhere outside your own machine, you have to assume it's compromised and treat removing it from history as a cleanup step, not the actual fix. After rotating the key, cleaning the history itself (with tools like git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner, or simply accepting it if the repo is small and early enough to just start history over) is worth doing for hygiene, but it is not a substitute for rotating the key, since anyone who already has a copy of the repo still has the old key regardless of what later happens to history.
questions.professionalAnswer: My very first move, before touching Git again at all, is going straight to the provider's dashboard and revoking that key, then generating a replacement. That's non-negotiable and has to happen immediately, because the instant that commit was pushed, I have to assume the key is compromised -- someone could have already seen it, scraped it, or cloned the repo in those few minutes. Only after the key is dead do I worry about cleanup: deleting the file in a new commit is fine for keeping the current state of the repo clean going forward, but I'm clear that it does nothing about the actual exposure, since the original commit with the real key is still sitting in history, fully retrievable by anyone who looks. If the repo and its history matter enough, I'd use a tool like git filter-repo to actually scrub the key out of every historical commit, but I treat that as hygiene on top of an already-rotated key, never as the fix itself.
commonMistakes: Deleting the file in a new commit and assuming that resolves the exposure
Rotating the key only after trying to clean up Git history, instead of rotating it first and immediately
Not realizing anyone who already pulled or cloned the repo still has the old commit with the key regardless of later history cleanup
Treating this as purely a Git problem instead of first and foremost a security incident requiring key rotation
keyPoints: The original commit with the key is still fully present in history even after a later deletion commit
Rotate (revoke and replace) the leaked key immediately -- this is the actual fix, not an optional extra step
History cleanup (filter-repo, BFG) is hygiene on top of rotation, not a substitute for it
Anyone who already cloned/pulled the repo before the fix still has the old key regardless of later history changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why deleting the file alone is insufficient
Identifies key rotation as the immediate, non-negotiable first step
Mentions history cleanup as a secondary hygiene step

questions.title: A pull request's CI check is failing
questions.prompt: You open a pull request and GitHub shows a red X next to a check called 'run-tests'. How would you investigate what actually failed, and what are the most common beginner-level reasons a check like this fails that have nothing to do with your actual feature logic?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is simply opening the failing check's details/logs directly from the pull request page -- GitHub shows the full output of whatever command the workflow ran, and that log almost always names the specific failing test or error near the end of the output, rather than requiring guesswork. Common beginner-level causes that have nothing to do with the actual feature's logic include: a missing or outdated dependency in requirements.txt that the CI environment doesn't have, since CI builds a clean environment from scratch rather than reusing whatever happens to already be installed on your own machine; an environment variable or secret the code expects that isn't configured in the CI environment; a test that passes locally but relies on something environment-specific, like a particular file path or time zone, that differs in CI; and simply not having run the test suite locally before pushing, so a straightforward, easily-caught failure only surfaces once CI runs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd click straight into the failing check's log rather than guessing, since GitHub Actions shows the full command output and the actual error or failing test name is almost always right there near the bottom. A few things I check first because they're the most common beginner trip-ups: did I actually add a new dependency to requirements.txt, or does it just happen to already be installed on my own machine locally; is there an environment variable or secret my code reads that simply isn't set up in the CI environment the same way it is on my machine; and, honestly, did I actually run the test suite locally before pushing at all, because a huge fraction of 'mystery' CI failures are just a test I'd have caught in ten seconds if I'd run it myself first. Once I've read the actual log and ruled those out, I treat it like any other test failure -- reproduce it, fix the actual code, and push again to re-trigger the check.
commonMistakes: Not opening the actual failing check's logs and instead guessing at what might be wrong
Forgetting CI builds a clean environment from scratch, so a locally-installed-but-unlisted dependency works locally but fails in CI
Assuming environment variables/secrets available locally are automatically available in the CI environment
Pushing without ever running the test suite locally first, letting an easily-caught failure show up only in CI
keyPoints: Open the failing check's actual log output first -- the specific failure is almost always named there
Missing dependencies in requirements.txt are a common cause, since CI builds a clean environment
Missing environment variables/secrets in the CI environment is another common cause
Run the test suite locally before pushing to catch easily-avoidable failures earlier

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes checking the actual CI logs as the first investigation step
Names at least two realistic beginner-level, non-logic causes
Clarity of the overall investigation approach

questions.title: A website won't load -- where do you even start
questions.prompt: A coworker says 'the website is down' and nothing else. Walk through the systematic troubleshooting methodology you'd actually use to narrow down the cause, rather than guessing at a fix immediately.
questions.modelAnswer: A sound methodology starts by reproducing and scoping the problem before touching anything: is it down for everyone or just this one coworker, and on what network -- that single question splits the investigation in two completely different directions (a local/individual issue vs. an actual outage). Next, work outward from the simplest, most likely layer: check whether the coworker's own device can reach other sites at all (ruling out their local network/ISP), then whether DNS resolves the site's name to an IP at all, then whether the server actually responds to a basic connection (ping, or a port check), and finally whether the application itself is returning a real HTTP response (via curl or a browser's network tab) rather than timing out or erroring. Jumping straight to 'restart the server' without this sequence risks fixing nothing, since the actual cause could just as easily be the coworker's own Wi-Fi or a DNS problem that a server restart would do nothing about.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd actually ask, before touching any system, is 'is it down for you only, or for everyone, and from what network?' -- that one question already splits this into two completely different investigations. If it's just this coworker, I'd have them try another site entirely to rule out their own connection, then check if the site's name even resolves for them. If it really is down more broadly, I'd work the same ladder myself: does the name resolve, does the server respond to a basic ping or port check, and finally does curl -v actually get an HTTP response or does it hang or return an error. I'd resist jumping to 'let's restart the server' as a first move, because without that sequence I genuinely don't know yet whether a restart would fix anything at all -- it might just be DNS, which a restart does nothing for.
commonMistakes: Jumping to a fix (restarting a server) before scoping whether the problem is isolated to one person or everyone
Not asking what network/device the reporting person is on, missing a purely local issue
Skipping straight to application-level investigation without first confirming basic reachability and DNS resolution
Treating a vague report as enough information to act on without first reproducing or narrowing it
keyPoints: First scope the problem: is it everyone or just this person, and from what network
Work outward from the simplest layer (local connectivity, DNS, basic reachability) toward the application
Don't act on a vague report without first narrowing down what's actually failing
A fix attempted before proper scoping risks solving nothing if the real cause is elsewhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes scoping the problem (one person vs. everyone) as the first step
Describes a logical, layer-by-layer investigation sequence
Clarity of the overall approach

questions.title: A firewall rule is blocking a connection you need open
questions.prompt: An application can't connect to a database on port 5432, and you suspect a firewall rule is blocking it rather than the database itself being down. How would you confirm that's actually the cause, as opposed to a DNS, routing, or application problem?
questions.modelAnswer: The key diagnostic is distinguishing a connection that's actively refused (the destination is reachable, but nothing is listening or something explicitly rejects it) from one that simply times out with no response at all (characteristic of a firewall silently dropping the traffic, as most security-conscious firewall configurations do rather than sending back an explicit rejection). A tool like telnet <host> 5432 or nc -zv <host> 5432 attempts a raw TCP connection to that specific port without any application-level protocol on top -- if it connects immediately, the port is open and the problem is elsewhere (likely in the application itself); if it hangs and eventually times out with no response, that's consistent with a firewall silently dropping the traffic; if it's actively and immediately refused, something is reachable but not listening on that port, which points to the database service itself rather than a firewall. Ruling out DNS first (confirming the hostname resolves to the expected IP) and routing (confirming basic ping/traceroute reachability to the host) narrows the field before concluding it's specifically a firewall rule.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first rule out DNS and basic routing -- does the hostname resolve to the IP I expect, and does a basic ping or traceroute even reach that host at all. Once those look fine, the actual test I'd run is nc -zv <host> 5432 (or telnet <host> 5432), which attempts a raw connection to exactly that port with nothing else going on. If it connects instantly, the port's open and the firewall isn't the problem -- something in the database or application itself is. If it just hangs and times out with no response at all, that's the classic signature of a firewall silently dropping the traffic rather than rejecting it outright, since most firewalls are configured to drop rather than send back an explicit 'connection refused.' An immediate, explicit refusal instead usually means the host is reachable but nothing's actually listening on that port, which points at the database service, not the firewall.
commonMistakes: Not distinguishing a timeout (consistent with a firewall silently dropping traffic) from an immediate refusal (consistent with nothing listening)
Skipping straight to blaming the firewall without first ruling out DNS and basic routing
Testing with a full application client instead of a raw TCP check, making it harder to isolate exactly where the failure occurs
Assuming a firewall issue without actually running a targeted test to confirm it
keyPoints: Rule out DNS and basic routing/reachability before concluding it's a firewall issue
A raw TCP check (nc -zv or telnet) to the specific port isolates the test from application-level complexity
A silent timeout is consistent with a firewall dropping traffic; an immediate refusal points to nothing listening on that port
Confirm, don't assume, which layer the failure is actually at before acting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes a targeted test to isolate the firewall as the cause
Correctly distinguishes a timeout from an active refusal
Mentions ruling out DNS/routing first

questions.title: 'Permission denied' when trying to run your own script
questions.prompt: You write a new script, deploy.sh, and run ./deploy.sh, but the shell prints 'Permission denied.' You're logged in as the file's owner. What's actually going on, and what command fixes it?
questions.modelAnswer: Being the file's owner and being able to execute it are two completely separate things in Linux -- ownership doesn't automatically grant execute permission, and a freshly created file typically defaults to a mode like 644 (rw-r--r--), which has no execute bit set for anyone, including the owner. Running ./deploy.sh specifically invokes it as an executable program, which requires the execute bit to be set on the file for whichever permission class applies to the current user. The fix is chmod +x deploy.sh, which adds the execute bit (for owner, group, and others, by default with the plain +x form), after which ./deploy.sh will actually run. This is different from a 'permission denied' caused by not being allowed to read the directory, or from running the script with bash deploy.sh instead, which doesn't require the execute bit at all since bash is reading and interpreting the file's contents directly rather than the kernel executing it as a program.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is ls -l deploy.sh, and I'd expect to see something like -rw-r--r--, with no x anywhere in the permission string -- that's almost always the actual cause here, not some deeper issue. Being the owner of a file doesn't automatically mean you can execute it; a new file typically starts with no execute bit set at all for anyone. The fix is just chmod +x deploy.sh, which adds execute permission, and then ./deploy.sh works. I'd also mention the workaround that doesn't require fixing permissions at all: bash deploy.sh runs the script by explicitly handing it to bash to interpret, which doesn't need the execute bit, but chmod +x is the actual fix if you want it to run as a normal executable going forward.
questions.example:
ls -l deploy.sh
# -rw-r--r--  1 alice  alice  120 Jan 5 10:00 deploy.sh   <- no x bit

chmod +x deploy.sh
ls -l deploy.sh
# -rwxr--r--  1 alice  alice  120 Jan 5 10:00 deploy.sh   <- now executable

./deploy.sh   # now runs
commonMistakes: Assuming file ownership automatically grants execute permission
Not checking ls -l first to actually confirm the execute bit is missing before guessing at other causes
Overusing chmod 777 as a blanket fix instead of the narrower, correct chmod +x
Not knowing bash deploy.sh is an alternative that bypasses the execute-bit requirement entirely
keyPoints: Ownership and execute permission are separate -- a new file often has no execute bit set by default
ls -l confirms whether the execute bit is actually missing
chmod +x deploy.sh adds execute permission and fixes the direct ./deploy.sh invocation
bash deploy.sh is an alternative that doesn't require the execute bit at all

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing execute bit as the cause
Provides the correct chmod fix
Mentions the diagnostic step (ls -l) or the bash-invocation alternative

questions.title: A process is pegging the CPU -- how do you find and handle it
questions.prompt: A Linux server feels sluggish and you suspect one runaway process is consuming most of the CPU. How would you identify exactly which process it is, and what are your options once you've found it?
questions.modelAnswer: top or htop (an improved, more readable version of top) gives a live, sortable view of running processes along with their current CPU and memory usage -- sorting by CPU usage (top's default sort, or pressing P) immediately surfaces whatever process is consuming the most CPU, along with its PID (process ID), which is needed for any further action. Once the offending PID is identified, the options are: investigate further (checking what the process actually is and whether its high usage is expected or a bug, using something like ps -p <PID> -f for details), or terminate it -- kill <PID> sends a graceful termination signal (SIGTERM) that gives the process a chance to shut down cleanly, while kill -9 <PID> (SIGKILL) forces it to stop immediately with no chance to clean up, which should generally be reserved for cases where a normal kill doesn't work, since skipping cleanup can leave things like temp files or database connections in a bad state.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open htop (or top if htop isn't installed) and sort by CPU, which immediately shows me the PID and command of whatever's actually eating the CPU at the top of the list.
