Before killing anything, I'd check what that process actually is with ps -p <PID> -f, because 'runaway process' could be a genuine bug worth investigating further, or it could be something expected (like a backup job that always spikes CPU briefly). If it genuinely needs to be stopped, I'd start with a plain kill <PID>, which sends SIGTERM and gives the process a chance to shut down and clean up after itself gracefully. I'd only reach for kill -9 <PID> if the plain kill doesn't actually stop it, since SIGKILL doesn't give the process any chance to clean up, which can leave things in a worse state than if I'd just waited a bit longer for a graceful shutdown.
questions.example:
htop   # sort by CPU, note the PID
ps -p 4821 -f   # inspect what that process actually is

kill 4821        # graceful (SIGTERM) -- try this first
kill -9 4821     # forceful (SIGKILL) -- only if the graceful kill doesn't work
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to kill -9 instead of trying a graceful kill first
Killing a process without first checking what it actually is and whether its CPU usage is expected
Not knowing how to sort top/htop by CPU usage to quickly find the offending process
Confusing the process name with its PID when trying to act on it
keyPoints: top/htop sorted by CPU usage quickly identifies the offending process and its PID
Investigate what the process actually is before deciding to kill it
kill (SIGTERM) attempts a graceful shutdown; kill -9 (SIGKILL) forces immediate termination with no cleanup
Try a graceful kill first; reserve SIGKILL for when that doesn't work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes identifying the process via top/htop
Correctly distinguishes graceful kill from SIGKILL and the order to try them
Mentions investigating the process before killing it

questions.title: A script works when run manually but fails under cron
questions.prompt: A backup script runs perfectly when you execute it yourself from the terminal, but silently fails every night when it's scheduled via cron. What are the most likely reasons for that gap, and how would you debug it?
questions.modelAnswer: The single most common cause is that cron runs jobs with a minimal environment -- a much smaller PATH and few or none of the environment variables your interactive shell has (set in files like .bashrc, which cron doesn't load) -- so a script that calls a command by name, assuming it's on PATH, or that relies on an environment variable you only ever set interactively, can fail under cron while working fine in your terminal. Other common causes include the script using a relative file path that happens to work from your terminal's current directory but doesn't resolve correctly from cron's default working directory, and the script's output (including errors) going nowhere, since cron by default only emails output to local mail delivery, which often isn't actually configured, making a real failure look like silent nothing happening. The fix for debugging is redirecting the cron job's output to a log file explicitly (so errors are actually visible), using absolute paths throughout the script instead of relying on PATH or relative paths, and explicitly sourcing or setting any environment variables the script needs inside the script itself rather than assuming they're inherited.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first suspicion is always environment differences -- cron runs with a stripped-down environment, not your interactive shell's environment, so if the script calls a command like aws or restic by name and relies on PATH including wherever that's installed, it can work fine in your terminal and fail completely under cron where PATH is much shorter. My first fix for debugging is making the cron entry redirect output to a log file -- something like 0 2 * * * /path/to/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 -- because by default cron's output often just goes nowhere useful, making a real error look like silent failure. Once I can actually see the error in that log, it's almost always either a 'command not found' confirming the PATH theory, or a relative path that doesn't resolve from cron's working directory. The long-term fix is using absolute paths for every command and file reference inside the script, and explicitly setting any needed environment variables at the top of the script itself instead of assuming they'll be inherited.
commonMistakes: Not knowing cron runs jobs in a minimal environment, missing PATH entries and variables an interactive shell has
Not redirecting cron's job output to a log file, making real errors invisible instead of investigating them
Using relative file paths or bare command names that only resolve correctly from an interactive shell's context
Assuming the script is simply broken rather than suspecting an environment difference first
keyPoints: cron runs with a minimal environment (short PATH, no interactive-shell variables)
Redirect cron job output to a log file to make real errors visible instead of silent
Use absolute paths for commands and files inside a script meant to run under cron
Explicitly set any needed environment variables inside the script rather than assuming inheritance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies cron's minimal environment as the likely cause
Describes a concrete debugging approach (logging output)
Names a correct preventive fix (absolute paths, explicit env vars)

questions.title: Debugging a Python script that crashes with a KeyError
questions.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "report.py", line 12, in <module>
    region = record['region']
KeyError: 'region'
questions.prompt: A Python script processing a list of records crashes partway through with the traceback shown above. Walk through how you'd actually diagnose and fix this, rather than just wrapping the line in a bare try/except to make the error go away.
questions.modelAnswer: The traceback already tells you precisely what's wrong and where -- a KeyError on 'region' at line 12 means some record in the list is missing the 'region' key entirely, and dict indexing with [] raises immediately on a missing key rather than returning a default. Just wrapping the line in a bare try/except would make the symptom disappear without answering the actual question of why some record is missing that key, and risks silently skipping or mishandling real data problems. A better diagnostic first step is printing or logging the specific record that caused the failure (which record index, and its actual keys) to understand whether this is expected (some records simply don't have a region, and should be handled with a sensible default) or a genuine data quality bug further upstream that should be fixed at the source. Once that's understood, the fix is either record.get('region', 'Unknown') to supply an explicit default for records that are legitimately missing the field, or a deliberate, specific except KeyError with logging if a missing region should actually be flagged and investigated rather than silently defaulted.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just slap a try/except around line 12 and move on -- that fixes the crash but tells me nothing about why a record is missing 'region' in the first place, and it might be hiding a real upstream data problem. My first move is adding a print or log right before that line showing the actual record that's failing, so I can see exactly what it does and doesn't have. If it turns out some records just legitimately don't have a region -- maybe that's a valid state for certain record types -- I'd switch to record.get('region', 'Unknown') so there's an explicit, intentional default instead of a crash. If it turns out this record SHOULD have had a region and doesn't, that's actually a bug somewhere upstream in how the data was produced, and I'd rather catch that loudly -- maybe with a specific except KeyError that logs the full record and re-raises or flags it -- than silently paper over it with a default that hides a real problem.
commonMistakes: Wrapping the failing line in a bare try/except without first understanding why the key is actually missing
Using a default value (.get()) everywhere without considering whether a missing key actually indicates a real upstream data bug
Not logging or printing the actual problematic record to understand the real cause
Fixing the symptom at the exact failing line instead of considering whether the real fix belongs further upstream
keyPoints: A KeyError traceback already names the exact missing key and the exact line -- read it before guessing
Investigate the specific record causing the failure before deciding on a fix
dict.get(key, default) supplies an intentional default when a missing key is a legitimate, expected case
Don't silently swallow the error with a bare except if a missing key might indicate a real upstream bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reads and explains what the traceback indicates
Describes a real diagnostic step before fixing (inspecting the actual record)
Proposes a fix that distinguishes 'legitimately missing' from 'real bug', not just a bare except

questions.title: A container exits immediately after docker run
questions.code:
$ docker run myapp
$ docker ps
# (empty -- no running containers)
questions.prompt: You run docker run myapp, and the container starts but immediately exits, with docker ps showing nothing running. Walk through how you'd investigate why, and name at least two common beginner causes.
questions.modelAnswer: The first diagnostic step is docker ps -a (showing all containers, including stopped ones) to find the exited container and see its exit code, followed by docker logs <container-id-or-name> to see exactly what the process printed before it stopped -- that log almost always contains the actual error or explanation. A core concept that explains many beginner cases is that a container stays running only as long as its main process (PID 1 inside the container) keeps running -- if that process finishes (even successfully) or crashes, the container stops immediately, regardless of what else might be installed inside the image. Common beginner causes include: the image's CMD/ENTRYPOINT running a short-lived command that naturally finishes quickly (like a one-off script) rather than a long-running server process, the main process crashing on startup due to a missing environment variable or config file it expected, or the container's command failing because a file it needed wasn't actually copied into the image during the build.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always docker ps -a, not just docker ps, since the stopped container is still there and its exit code is genuinely informative -- a 0 means the process finished successfully but just didn't keep running, anything else usually means it crashed. Then docker logs <container-id> to see exactly what that process printed right before stopping, which in my experience explains the problem the large majority of the time. The core thing to remember is a container only lives as long as its main process does -- if the Dockerfile's CMD is something that naturally finishes in a second, like a quick script rather than a server that listens and blocks, the container exits the moment that script finishes, and that's completely expected Docker behavior, not a bug. The other common beginner trap is the main process crashing on startup because it's missing an environment variable or a config file it expected to find, which the logs will usually spell out directly if you actually read them.
commonMistakes: Checking only docker ps instead of docker ps -a, missing the stopped container entirely
Not checking docker logs, which almost always contains the actual explanation
Not understanding that a container exits the moment its main process finishes or crashes, regardless of what else is in the image
Assuming the container crashed when it actually just ran a short-lived command successfully and had nothing left to keep it alive
keyPoints: docker ps -a shows stopped containers and their exit codes; docker logs shows what the process actually printed
A container's lifetime is tied directly to its main (PID 1) process -- it stops the moment that process exits
A short-lived CMD finishing naturally is a common, expected cause, not necessarily a crash
A missing environment variable or config file causing the main process to crash on startup is another common cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes docker ps -a and docker logs as the correct investigation steps
Correctly explains that a container's lifetime is tied to its main process
Names at least two realistic, distinct common causes

questions.title: Choosing a branching strategy for a small team
questions.prompt: You're setting up Git workflow conventions for a 4-person team building an application together. Would you recommend a Git Flow-style strategy with long-lived develop/release branches, or a simpler trunk-based approach with short-lived feature branches off main? What would change your answer?
questions.modelAnswer: For a small, 4-person team, trunk-based development -- short-lived feature branches that branch off main, get reviewed quickly, and merge back within a day or two -- is almost always the better fit: Git Flow's additional long-lived branches (develop, release, hotfix) add real process overhead -- more branches to keep in sync, more merge points where things can drift -- that pays off mainly at a scale where multiple release versions genuinely need to be maintained in parallel, which a small team building one continuously-deployed application typically doesn't need. The deciding factor that would change the answer is whether the team needs to support multiple released versions simultaneously (for example, maintaining a stable production release while a next major version is developed separately) -- that's the scenario Git Flow's structure is actually built for, and a team in that situation benefits from the extra branches even at a small headcount.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a 4-person team, I'd recommend trunk-based: short-lived feature branches off main, a pull request and quick review, then merge back within a day or two, keeping main always close to deployable. Git Flow's extra branches -- develop, release, hotfix -- exist to solve a problem this team likely doesn't have yet: needing to maintain multiple released versions of the software at the same time. With 4 people shipping one continuously deployed application, that extra branch structure is mostly overhead -- more places for things to get out of sync, more process to remember -- without a corresponding benefit. The one thing that would flip my recommendation is if this team suddenly needed to support, say, an older stable release for some customers while actively developing a new major version for others -- that's genuinely the situation Git Flow's structure is designed around, and at that point the extra discipline becomes worth it even for a small team.
commonMistakes: Recommending Git Flow by default regardless of team size or actual release-management needs
Not identifying the real deciding factor -- supporting multiple released versions in parallel
Assuming trunk-based development means no code review or no branches at all, rather than short-lived ones
Treating this as a purely technical choice without considering the team's actual workflow and deployment cadence
keyPoints: Trunk-based development (short-lived branches off main) suits most small teams shipping one continuously deployed app
Git Flow's long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches solve a specific problem: maintaining multiple released versions in parallel
The deciding factor is whether multiple versions genuinely need parallel maintenance, not team size alone
Overhead from extra long-lived branches isn't justified without that parallel-version need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a clear, justified recommendation for this team's situation
Correctly characterizes what Git Flow's structure is actually for
Identifies the correct deciding factor that would change the answer

questions.title: Forking workflow vs. direct branch-and-PR workflow
questions.prompt: When would you use the forking workflow (each contributor forks the repo to their own account) instead of giving every contributor direct push access to branch off the main repository? What's actually different about the two, mechanically?
questions.modelAnswer: In the direct workflow, every contributor has push access to the same shared repository and creates branches directly inside it, opening pull requests from branch to branch within that one repo. In the forking workflow, a contributor doesn't have push access to the original repository at all -- they create their own independent copy (a fork) under their own account, push branches and commits to that fork, and open a pull request from their fork's branch back to the original repository, which the original repository's maintainers then choose to accept. The forking workflow exists specifically for situations where you can't or shouldn't give direct push access to every contributor: open-source projects accepting contributions from the general public being the classic case, since granting push access to an unknown, unvetted public contributor isn't reasonable, but a fork-and-PR contribution still gives the maintainers full review and control before anything merges. For a small internal team where everyone is already trusted and has legitimate reasons to push, the direct branch-and-PR workflow is simpler and has no real downside -- forking adds a layer of indirection with no corresponding benefit in that situation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanical difference is about where the contributor's branch actually lives. In the direct model, I branch inside the same shared repository everyone already has push access to. In the forking model, I don't have push access to the original repo at all -- I create my own full copy of it under my own account, push my branch there, and then open a pull request from my fork back to the original repo, which its maintainers review and merge (or don't) entirely at their discretion. I'd reach for forking specifically for open-source-style situations -- contributing to a public project I don't work for, where it would be unreasonable for the maintainers to hand out push access to every random contributor. For an internal team of people who are already trusted collaborators, I'd skip forking entirely and just use direct branches off the shared repo with pull requests -- forking there is extra indirection with no real security or workflow benefit.
commonMistakes: Not understanding that forking creates an entirely separate copy of the repository under the contributor's own account
Using the forking workflow for a trusted internal team where it adds unnecessary indirection
Assuming a pull request from a fork works mechanically differently from a pull request between branches in the same repo, when the review/merge process is otherwise similar
Not identifying open-source/untrusted-contributor access control as the real reason forking exists
keyPoints: Direct workflow: contributors push branches directly to the shared repository
Forking workflow: contributors push to their own separate copy, then PR back to the original repo
Forking exists to let maintainers accept contributions without granting push access to untrusted/unknown contributors
For a trusted internal team, direct branching is simpler with no real downside

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanical difference between the two workflows
Correctly identifies when forking is actually warranted
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Load balancer vs. reverse proxy: when do you actually need which
questions.prompt: You have one web application running on a single server, and you're designing for a near-future where it needs to scale to multiple server instances. Would you put a reverse proxy in front of it now, a load balancer, both, or neither? Explain the reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer: A reverse proxy sits in front of one or more backend servers and handles things like TLS termination, caching, and request routing/rewriting, but it doesn't inherently distribute traffic across multiple equivalent backend instances -- that's specifically what a load balancer does, distributing incoming requests across multiple servers running the same application so no single instance is overwhelmed. For a single server today, a reverse proxy makes sense on its own merits (TLS termination, basic security hardening, serving static assets efficiently) even before scaling is needed. Many load balancers are actually implemented as a specific configuration of a reverse proxy (or the same software, like nginx or HAProxy, can do both jobs), so adding a reverse proxy now that's capable of being reconfigured into a load-balancing role later is a reasonable, forward-looking choice -- but a load balancer by itself is pointless with only one backend server, since there's nothing to balance across yet.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put a reverse proxy in front of the single server now, mainly for TLS termination and so the application itself doesn't need to deal with certificates directly, plus the basic security benefit of not exposing the application server straight to the internet. I wouldn't add a load balancer yet, though, because with exactly one backend instance there's nothing to actually balance across -- it would just be an extra hop doing nothing useful. The reason this isn't wasted effort for the future is that the same software, like nginx or HAProxy, that's acting as my reverse proxy today can be reconfigured into a load balancer later with a config change once there are multiple backend instances to route across -- so I'm not throwing away the reverse-proxy investment when scaling actually happens, I'm just expanding its config.
commonMistakes: Treating 'reverse proxy' and 'load balancer' as interchangeable terms for the same thing
Adding a load balancer with only one backend instance, where there's nothing to distribute across yet
Not recognizing the same software can serve as both a reverse proxy and, later, a load balancer
Skipping a reverse proxy entirely for a single server, missing its TLS-termination and security benefits even pre-scale
keyPoints: A reverse proxy handles TLS termination, caching, and routing in front of backend server(s)
A load balancer specifically distributes traffic across multiple equivalent backend instances
A load balancer provides no benefit with only one backend server
The same software (nginx, HAProxy) can serve as a reverse proxy now and be reconfigured as a load balancer later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes a reverse proxy from a load balancer
Gives a justified recommendation for the single-server-today scenario
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Choosing IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS for a small team's new app
questions.prompt: A 3-person startup wants to build and host a new web application quickly, without hiring anyone dedicated to managing servers. Would you recommend IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS for hosting the application itself, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) hands you raw virtual machines, networking, and storage, but you're still responsible for the operating system, runtime, patching, and scaling logic yourself -- that's a reasonable choice when you need deep control, but it directly conflicts with 'no one dedicated to managing servers.' SaaS is fully built, ready-to-use software (like a CRM) that you don't customize at the code level, which doesn't fit 'build a new web application' at all, since there's no application code to deploy into a SaaS product. PaaS (Platform as a Service) sits in between: the provider manages the underlying servers, operating system, and runtime, while you deploy your own application code directly, typically via a simple deploy command or Git push, which fits this scenario well -- a small team gets to focus on writing their application rather than operating infrastructure, at some cost in lower-level control and typically a higher per-resource price than raw IaaS.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recommend PaaS. IaaS would technically work, but 'no one dedicated to managing servers' is a direct conflict with IaaS's whole model, where you're still responsible for patching the OS, configuring the runtime, and handling scaling yourself -- that's real ongoing operational work this team explicitly doesn't want to take on. SaaS doesn't fit at all here, since the whole point is building a new application, and SaaS is pre-built software you use, not a platform you deploy custom code onto. PaaS is the actual sweet spot: something like a managed app-hosting platform where the team pushes their code and the platform handles the server, OS, and runtime underneath. It costs more per unit of compute than doing the same thing on raw IaaS and gives up some low-level control, but for a 3-person team that wants to spend their limited time writing the application instead of operating infrastructure, that tradeoff is clearly worth it.
commonMistakes: Recommending IaaS without acknowledging it still requires ongoing server/OS management the team explicitly wants to avoid
Confusing SaaS (pre-built software) with a platform for deploying custom application code
Not naming the actual tradeoff (less control, higher relative cost) that comes with choosing PaaS
Treating the three models as differing only in cost, rather than in who manages what layer
keyPoints: IaaS: raw infrastructure, you manage OS/runtime/patching/scaling yourself
PaaS: provider manages the OS/runtime, you deploy your own application code
SaaS: fully built software you use, not a platform for your own custom code
For a small team avoiding server management, PaaS fits best despite less low-level control and higher relative cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
Gives a justified recommendation fitting this team's actual constraint
Names the real tradeoff involved in that recommendation

questions.title: Choosing a Linux distribution for a new production server
questions.prompt: Your team is setting up a new production server and hasn't picked a Linux distribution yet. What factors would actually drive that decision, and would you default to whatever's newest and most popular?
questions.modelAnswer: The decision shouldn't default to 'whatever's newest and trendiest' -- for a production server, the main factors are: how long the distribution's long-term support (LTS) release is actually maintained with security patches (Ubuntu LTS releases get around 5 years, for example, which matters for a server you don't want to re-provision constantly just to stay patched), what the team already has operational experience with (consistency across a team's servers reduces the chance of a mistake from unfamiliar tooling under pressure), and what the existing software/tooling the team depends on officially supports or is tested against, since using an unsupported distribution for a given piece of software can mean fighting avoidable compatibility issues. Picking the newest release available, rather than its most recent LTS version, is usually the wrong call for a server that needs to stay stable and patched for years without being rebuilt from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just grab whatever's newest. The first question I'd actually ask is what the team already runs and knows -- if everyone's used to Ubuntu, introducing a totally different distribution for one new server adds unfamiliarity risk with no real benefit. Then I'd check the LTS support window, since a production server needs security patches for years without a full rebuild, and I'd specifically pick the LTS release, not the latest non-LTS version, which typically has a much shorter support window. Finally, I'd check what the actual software we're running on this server officially supports or is tested against -- running something on an unsupported distribution just because it's newer is exactly the kind of decision that causes an avoidable compatibility problem six months later that nobody budgeted time for.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the newest available release instead of a long-term-support version meant for production stability
Not considering the team's existing operational familiarity with a given distribution
Ignoring what the actual software stack officially supports or has been tested against
Treating distribution choice as a purely personal-preference decision rather than an operational one
keyPoints: LTS support window matters for a production server that needs years of patches without a full rebuild
Team familiarity with a distribution reduces operational risk versus introducing something unfamiliar
Check what the actual software stack officially supports, rather than assuming any distro works equally well
Newest/most popular isn't automatically the right choice for a production server

Correctly identifies team familiarity and software-support compatibility as factors
Explicitly rejects 'newest/most popular' as the default criterion

questions.title: cron vs. systemd timers for scheduling a job
questions.prompt: You need to schedule a nightly backup job on a modern Linux server that uses systemd. Would you use a traditional cron job or a systemd timer, and what would actually change your answer?
questions.modelAnswer: cron is simpler to set up for a basic, fixed schedule -- a single line in a crontab is enough, and it's familiar to almost everyone with any Linux experience. A systemd timer takes more setup (a .timer unit paired with a .service unit) but integrates with systemd's broader feature set: better logging through journalctl tied to the specific job, the ability to express dependencies on other systemd units (like waiting for a network-mounted drive to be ready before running), and features like automatically catching up a missed run if the system was powered off at the scheduled time. For a simple, single nightly job with no dependencies and no need for that deeper integration, cron is often perfectly sufficient and simpler to reason about. The deciding factor that would push toward a systemd timer instead is needing one of its specific extra capabilities -- dependency ordering on other units, better per-job log integration, or missed-run catch-up behavior -- rather than complexity for its own sake.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a simple nightly backup with no dependencies, I'd actually default to cron -- it's one line, everyone on the team already understands it, and a systemd timer's extra setup (a separate .timer and .service unit pair) doesn't buy anything extra for a job this simple. What would change my answer is needing something systemd timers specifically do better: if the backup job depends on a network drive being mounted first, a systemd timer can express that dependency directly against another systemd unit, where cron has no concept of 'wait for this other thing to be ready.' I'd also lean toward a systemd timer if I specifically need journalctl's per-job logging integration, or if I need the job to automatically run on catch-up if the server happened to be off at the scheduled time, which cron doesn't handle on its own. Without one of those specific needs, I don't reach for the extra complexity just because it's the newer option.
commonMistakes: Assuming a systemd timer is strictly 'better' and should always be preferred over cron just because it's newer
Not naming a concrete systemd-timer capability (dependency ordering, missed-run catch-up, journalctl integration) that would actually justify the extra complexity
Choosing cron purely out of habit without acknowledging where it genuinely falls short
Treating this as a purely stylistic choice rather than one driven by the job's actual requirements
keyPoints: cron is simpler for a basic, fixed, dependency-free schedule
systemd timers integrate with unit dependencies, journalctl logging, and missed-run catch-up
The deciding factor is needing one of those specific systemd-timer capabilities, not complexity for its own sake
Neither option is universally 'better' -- the choice depends on the job's actual requirements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly contrasts cron's simplicity with systemd timers' extra capabilities
Names a concrete deciding factor that would change the recommendation
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Bash or Python: choosing the right tool for an automation task
questions.prompt: You need to automate a task that renames a batch of files based on a pattern, and a separate task that calls a REST API, parses the JSON response, and makes a decision based on several of its fields. Would you write each one in Bash or Python, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The file-renaming task is a strong fit for Bash: it's fundamentally about chaining together existing command-line tools (like a for loop with mv, or rename) that are already designed for exactly this kind of filesystem operation, and Bash's whole design center is gluing commands together simply. The REST API task is a much better fit for Python: Bash can technically call an API with curl, but parsing a JSON response's nested structure and making decisions based on multiple fields is clumsy and fragile in Bash's string-oriented world, whereas Python's requests library and built-in json module handle both naturally, and Python's actual data structures (dicts, conditionals, proper error handling) make multi-field decision logic far more maintainable and less error-prone than trying to do the equivalent with grep/sed/awk text parsing. The general rule of thumb: Bash is good for gluing together existing commands and simple file/text operations; Python is the better choice once there's real data structure to parse or non-trivial logic to express.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the renaming task in Bash -- it's exactly the kind of job Bash is built for, looping over files and calling mv in a pattern, with no real data structures or complex logic involved. For the API task, I'd reach for Python without much debate: the moment I'm parsing a JSON response with nested fields and making a decision based on several of them together, Python's json module and normal dict/conditional logic are just dramatically more maintainable than trying to pull the same thing apart with grep and sed against curl's raw text output. My actual rule of thumb is: if the task is mostly 'run this command, then that command, in sequence,' Bash is fine and often simpler. The moment there's real data to parse or non-trivial decision logic involving multiple pieces of that data, I switch to Python, because that's where Bash's lack of real data structures starts actively working against me instead of just being a minor inconvenience.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to one language for every automation task regardless of what the task actually involves
Trying to parse nested JSON with grep/sed/awk instead of recognizing that's exactly where Python's json module is the better tool
Writing a simple file-renaming loop in Python when Bash would be simpler and just as effective
Not articulating a clear, reusable rule of thumb for the choice, beyond personal preference
keyPoints: Bash fits simple filesystem/command-chaining tasks like batch file renaming
Python fits tasks involving structured data (JSON) and non-trivial multi-field decision logic
Parsing nested JSON with grep/sed/awk is fragile compared to Python's json module and real data structures
Rule of thumb: command-chaining favors Bash; real data/logic favors Python

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends Bash for the file-renaming task with justification
Correctly recommends Python for the API/JSON task with justification
States a clear, reusable rule of thumb for the choice

questions.title: Storing secrets for a small automation script: env vars vs. a config file
questions.prompt: You're writing a small automation script that needs an API key to call a cloud provider's API. Would you hardcode the key in the script, put it in a plain config file checked into Git, store it in an environment variable, or something else? Walk through the reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer: Hardcoding the key directly in the script is the worst option -- it ends up committed to Git history the moment the script is checked in, and anyone with repo access (or anyone the repo is ever shared with) gets the real key. A plain config file checked into Git has exactly the same problem -- it's still a real secret sitting in version control history, just moved to a different file. An environment variable read at runtime (os.environ['API_KEY'] in Python, or $API_KEY in Bash) keeps the actual secret value out of the script and out of Git entirely -- the script only ever contains a reference to a variable name, and the real value is supplied separately, typically via a .env file that's explicitly excluded with .gitignore, or injected directly by whatever system runs the script (a CI/CD pipeline's secrets store, for example). For anything beyond a personal script, a dedicated secrets manager (like a cloud provider's own secret store) is an even better option than a local .env file, since it adds access control and auditing, but environment variables sourced from a gitignored file are a reasonable, common baseline for a small automation script.
questions.professionalAnswer: I would not hardcode the key in the script, and I would not put it in a plain config file that gets checked into Git either -- those are functionally the same mistake, just in a different file, and either way the real secret ends up sitting in Git history forever once committed. I'd read it from an environment variable instead -- os.environ['API_KEY'] in the script itself, with the actual value supplied through a .env file that's explicitly listed in .gitignore, or set directly by whatever's actually running the script, like a CI pipeline's own secrets feature. That way the script that gets committed to Git only ever references a variable name, never the real value. If this were growing beyond a personal script into something a team relies on, I'd push further toward an actual secrets manager rather than a local .env file, since that adds real access control and an audit trail of who accessed the secret and when, which a plain .env file on someone's laptop doesn't give you at all.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the secret directly in the script, guaranteeing it ends up in Git history once committed
Treating a plain config file checked into Git as meaningfully safer than hardcoding -- it isn't
Forgetting to add a .env file to .gitignore, defeating the whole purpose of keeping it out of the script
Not considering a dedicated secrets manager once the script matters beyond personal, one-off use
keyPoints: Hardcoding a secret in the script or in a committed config file both end up exposing it in Git history
Environment variables keep the real secret value out of the script and out of version control
A .env file supplying those variables must itself be excluded via .gitignore
A dedicated secrets manager is a stronger option than a local .env file once the script matters beyond personal use

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects hardcoding and a Git-committed config file
Correctly recommends environment variables with a gitignored source
Mentions a secrets manager as a stronger option at larger scale

questions.title: What belongs in the image vs. what belongs in a mounted volume
questions.prompt: You're containerizing an application that writes log files and stores uploaded user files on disk. Would you let those write to the container's own filesystem, or mount a volume for them? Walk through the reasoning, including what happens to each option when the container is removed.
questions.modelAnswer: A container's own writable layer is tied to that specific container's lifecycle -- when the container is removed (docker rm), everything written to its writable layer, including logs and uploaded files that were never put in a volume, is permanently gone with it. A volume is storage that exists independently of any one container's lifecycle -- it can be mounted into a container, survive that container being removed or replaced, and be re-mounted into a brand-new container started from the same image. For uploaded user files specifically, losing them the moment a container is removed or replaced (which happens routinely during a normal deployment/update) would be a real data-loss bug, so those absolutely belong in a volume, not the container's own filesystem. Logs are a similar case for persistence, though in practice many setups instead have the application write logs to stdout/stderr and let Docker's own logging driver or an external log-collection tool handle them, rather than relying on a file inside the container (or even a volume) at all -- the deciding principle either way is the same: anything that needs to outlive a specific container instance doesn't belong only in that container's own writable layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd mount a volume for the uploaded user files, without question -- if I let them write to the container's own filesystem and then that container gets removed during a normal deployment update, which happens routinely, those files are just gone. A volume exists independently of any single container's lifecycle, so I can remove and replace the container entirely and the volume's data is still there to mount into the new one. For logs, I'd actually lean toward having the application just write to stdout/stderr and let Docker's logging driver (or whatever log aggregation tool we're using) capture that externally, rather than writing to a file inside the container or even a volume -- that's a more common modern pattern and keeps the container itself fully disposable. The principle either way is the same: if data needs to survive past this one specific container instance being replaced, it does not belong solely in that container's own writable layer.
commonMistakes: Letting persistent user data write only to the container's own filesystem, losing it whenever the container is removed
Not understanding that a container's writable layer is deleted along with the container itself
Assuming a volume is part of the image rather than storage that exists independently of any specific container
Not considering stdout/stderr plus a logging driver as the more common modern approach for logs specifically
keyPoints: A container's own writable layer is deleted when the container is removed
A volume exists independently of any single container's lifecycle and can be re-mounted into a new container
Persistent user data (like uploads) must go in a volume, not the container's own filesystem
Logs are often better handled via stdout/stderr plus a logging driver than a file inside the container

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what happens to each option when the container is removed
Correctly recommends a volume for persistent user data with justification
Mentions a reasonable approach for logs specifically

questions.title: Multi-stage builds vs. a single-stage Dockerfile
questions.prompt: Your application needs to be compiled from source before it can run, and the build process requires a full set of compilers and build tools that the running application itself never needs. Would you use a single-stage Dockerfile or a multi-stage build, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: A single-stage Dockerfile that installs the full build toolchain, compiles the application, and then runs it leaves every one of those build-time-only tools sitting in the final image -- compilers, build caches, and intermediate artifacts that the running application never actually needs, all adding to the image's size and its attack surface for no runtime benefit. A multi-stage build splits this into separate stages: an early stage (FROM <build-image> AS builder) that has the full toolchain and actually compiles the application, and a later, final stage that starts fresh from a minimal base image and uses COPY --from=builder to pull only the specific compiled output (a binary, a built set of static files) from the first stage, discarding everything else that stage used along the way. The result is a final image containing only what's actually needed to run the application, meaningfully smaller and with a smaller attack surface than if the build toolchain were carried all the way through.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use a multi-stage build here without much hesitation. If I compile everything in a single stage that also has to run the application, the final image is stuck carrying every compiler and build tool I only needed for a few minutes during the build, forever, even though the running application has zero use for any of it afterward -- that's wasted size and genuinely unnecessary attack surface in production. With a multi-stage build, I'd have one stage FROM a full build image that installs the toolchain and compiles the app, and then a second, final stage that starts fresh FROM a minimal runtime base image and uses COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist to grab just the compiled output from the first stage. Everything else the build stage touched -- compilers, intermediate files, build caches -- never makes it into the final image at all, since that stage is simply discarded once its output has been copied out.
questions.example:
FROM node:20 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install && npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
commonMistakes: Using a single-stage Dockerfile that leaves the entire build toolchain in the final runtime image
Not using COPY --from=<stage> to pull only the needed build output into the final stage
Starting the final stage from the same large build image instead of a minimal runtime-appropriate base image
Not recognizing the build-time-only tools add both unnecessary size and unnecessary attack surface in production
keyPoints: A single-stage build leaves the entire build toolchain in the final image, unused at runtime
A multi-stage build uses an early stage for compiling and a separate final stage for running
COPY --from=<stage> pulls only the needed build output into the final, minimal stage
The result is a smaller final image with less unnecessary attack surface

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends a multi-stage build with justification
Correctly explains the mechanics (build stage, COPY --from, minimal final stage)
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the deployment script for the staging environment and started testing the rollback path. Today I'm wiring up the health check so a bad deploy gets flagged automatically instead of failing silently. I'm blocked on getting access to the staging server, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real task instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.
commonMistakes: Treating stand-up like a status report to a manager instead of the team syncing with itself
Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward
keyPoints: Daily Scrum/stand-up is short, time-boxed, and team-to-team, not a report to a manager
Typical shape: what I did, what I'm doing next, what's blocking me
Name specific work, not vague progress statements
Surface blockers immediately; save detailed discussion for after stand-up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a stand-up is and its purpose
Gives a specific, well-structured example of what to say
Avoids the common vague-status-report trap

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.
commonMistakes: Quietly grinding on a ticket without flagging it, assuming asking for help makes you look unprepared
Mislabeling 'off track' (just taking longer) as 'blocked' when there's still personal progress possible
Waiting until the next stand-up to mention a blocker instead of flagging it the moment it's identified
Flagging a blocker vaguely instead of saying specifically what's needed to unblock it
keyPoints: Off Track: work is simply taking longer than planned, more time/closer look resolves it
Blocked: a hard stop entirely outside your control -- no amount of personal effort moves it forward
The test: is there anything I can still do myself right now? If no, you're blocked
Flag a blocker immediately and specifically, not quietly or vaguely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Off Track from Blocked
Gives a usable decision test for telling them apart
Describes a clear, prompt way to communicate a real blocker

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole feature and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the system each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire feature was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the system, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.
commonMistakes: Explaining Agile/Waterfall in the abstract without connecting it to why it benefits this stakeholder specifically
Implying sprints mean nothing gets fully finished, instead of explaining a sprint still produces a real, shippable increment
Being dismissive of the stakeholder's preference instead of explaining the real trade-off
Using unexplained jargon (backlog, increment, retrospective) instead of plain language
keyPoints: Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements but surfaces mistakes late and expensively
Agile's short cycles let the stakeholder react to real progress every 1-2 weeks, catching misunderstandings early
Connect the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest, not an abstract process lecture
Each sprint still produces a real, working increment, not an unfinished fragment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains the Agile vs. Waterfall trade-off
Connects the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest
Communicates without unexplained jargon

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a deployment, a customer reports that a feature they rely on has been silently failing all morning. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the customer-facing team while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did last night's deployment actually complete successfully, are there obvious errors in the logs -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the team they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's deployment actually complete, or did it fail silently partway through? If the deployment looks fine, I'd check the application and service logs around the time the failures started, narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the fix is confirmed instead of acknowledging the report and giving a timeframe while still investigating
Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the deployment actually succeed)
Investigating only the symptom without checking whether the issue actually originates further upstream
Not giving a concrete time to expect an update, leaving the customer-facing team to wonder if it's been forgotten
keyPoints: Communicate an acknowledgment and a timeframe immediately, don't wait for the fix to say anything
Investigate by narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source
Check the simplest explanation first (did the deployment actually succeed) before assuming something complex
Follow up with a clear explanation once the cause is found, not just a silent fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical investigation approach, working from symptom back to source
Correctly emphasizes communicating early, before the cause is known
Clarity and professionalism of the communication described

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A manager emails you: 'People keep asking me for a status update on deployments by email. I need something that shows deployment status automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a team member, I want a dashboard showing current deployment status, so that I can check it myself without emailing the manager.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects a deployment's status within one minute of it changing, with no manual steps' and 'each environment (dev/staging/prod) is shown separately.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a deployment fails. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the manager directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a team member, I want a dashboard showing current deployment status, so that I can check it myself without emailing the manager.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects a status change within one minute, with no manual steps' and 'shows dev, staging, and prod separately.' The thing I'd specifically flag before building anything is that the email never says what should happen if a deployment fails -- show it as red immediately, send a notification, or just leave it to be noticed on the dashboard? I'd either ask the manager directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong after launch.
commonMistakes: Starting to build directly from the vague email instead of writing a structured user story first
Writing a user story with no acceptance criteria, leaving 'done' undefined
Silently guessing at an ambiguous detail (like the failure case) instead of asking or explicitly documenting the judgment call
Writing acceptance criteria that aren't actually checkable ('looks good') instead of specific and testable
keyPoints: User story shape: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria must be specific and checkable, not vague
Explicitly surface and resolve ambiguous details (like the failure-case edge case) before building
A story isn't ready to build until its acceptance criteria are defined

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly-shaped user story
Writes specific, checkable acceptance criteria
Identifies and resolves an ambiguous detail from the original request

questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior engineer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in a project, I couldn't get a script's scheduled run to actually trigger, and I'd already tried checking the schedule syntax and rereading the tool's docs with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced teammate a specific question -- 'the job is scheduled but it's never actually firing, here's the config and here's what I've already checked' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out the scheduler's service wasn't even running on that box. Result: once I started the service and confirmed it, the job began firing on schedule, and I started checking that the relevant service was actually running by default on everything I set up since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

Tells a specific, real story using STAR

questions.title: Why move from a support/helpdesk role toward DevOps
questions.prompt: You've been working in IT support or a helpdesk role. What's actually motivating you to grow into a DevOps Engineer role, and what have you been doing to build toward that?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is specific about what actually changes between the two roles, not just a vague sense that DevOps 'sounds like a step up.' A support role typically reacts to problems after they've already surfaced for an end user, working within systems someone else built and configured. A DevOps Engineer takes more ownership further upstream -- automating the setup and deployment of the systems themselves, building the pipelines and infrastructure that prevent whole categories of problems from reaching a user in the first place, and being responsible for reliability proactively, not just responding to tickets. A credible motivation names a specific experience that revealed that gap -- for example, repeatedly fixing the same manual issue by hand and wanting to be the person who automates it away instead of just the person who keeps fixing it. The second half of the answer should show concrete action already taken, not just intention -- specific skills being built (scripting, Linux administration, containers) rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific rather than giving the generic 'I want to grow' answer. What actually pushed me toward this was hitting a point, a few times, where I'd fix the exact same issue by hand for the third or fourth time -- restarting a service, re-running a setup step -- and I realized the real fix wasn't doing it faster by hand, it was making sure it never needed a human to do it at all. I kept having to file that as 'just how it is' and move on, and I realized I wanted to be the person who could actually automate that away. So I've been deliberately building the skills that sit upstream of where I was working before -- going deeper into Linux administration and shell scripting, learning how containers package an application so it behaves the same way everywhere, and understanding how a deployment pipeline actually works end to end -- rather than just saying I want the title.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer about wanting to 'grow' without naming the actual difference between the two roles
Describing DevOps as just 'more advanced IT support' instead of upstream automation and reliability ownership
Stating interest without describing any concrete action already taken toward it
Not having a specific, real experience that motivated the shift
keyPoints: Names the real distinction: support reacts to problems after they surface; DevOps automates to prevent them upstream
Motivation should come from a specific, real experience, not a vague sense of career progression
Shows concrete action already taken (specific skills being built), not just stated intention
Avoids treating DevOps as simply 'more advanced IT support'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two roles
Gives a specific, credible motivation
Describes concrete action already taken

questions.title: Responding to a pull request sent back for changes
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a teammate reviewed your work -- a script, a pipeline config, or a Dockerfile -- and sent it back with specific changes requested. How did you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing professionalism and how a candidate handles feedback, not a request for a technical fact. A strong answer first frames code review correctly: it happens before anything is allowed to merge, as a normal second set of eyes on the approach -- not a personal judgment, and it's completely normal for a reviewer to send work back before it merges. The answer should use the STAR structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result), with Action describing reading the specific feedback carefully, asking a clarifying question if the reasoning wasn't obvious rather than assuming or arguing, making the requested change (or explaining a respectful disagreement if there was a good reason), and re-requesting review. Result should state the concrete outcome -- the change was approved and merged, and ideally what was learned or changed going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story rather than describe my attitude toward feedback in general. Situation: on an automation script I wrote, a reviewer flagged that I was hardcoding a credential directly in the script instead of reading it from an environment variable. Task: I needed to understand why that mattered and fix it properly, not just make the comment go away. Action: I asked the reviewer to walk me through the actual risk, since I hadn't thought past 'it works,' then I pulled the credential out into an environment variable and updated the script to read it from there, and re-requested review with a short note explaining what I'd changed and why. Result: it was approved on the second pass, and I started checking every script I wrote after that for hardcoded secrets by default, which is the kind of habit a good review catches before it becomes a real production incident.
commonMistakes: Taking review feedback personally instead of treating it as a normal part of the process
Making the requested change without understanding why it was requested
Arguing defensively instead of asking a clarifying question when the reasoning isn't clear
Describing review feedback in general terms instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Code review happens before merge -- it's a normal second set of eyes, not a personal judgment
Read specific feedback carefully; ask a clarifying question if the reasoning isn't obvious
Make the change (or explain a respectful disagreement), then re-request review
Use STAR and state the concrete Result -- what happened after the change was made

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames review feedback as a normal part of the process, not a personal setback
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result

questions.title: Knowing when to escalate a production incident you can't yet solve
questions.prompt: In your first month as a junior DevOps engineer, you're paged because a production server's CPU is pegged and several applications are reporting timeouts. You have some ideas but you're not fully confident you've found the actual cause. How do you decide whether to keep investigating on your own or escalate, and how would you escalate without it looking like you can't do the job?
questions.modelAnswer: This tests judgment about risk and communication, not raw troubleshooting skill. The deciding factor shouldn't be ego (will escalating make me look bad) -- it should be the actual business impact and how much time has already passed: a production-wide incident actively affecting multiple applications has a low tolerance for a junior engineer quietly investigating alone for an extended period on a hunch. A reasonable approach is time-boxing the initial investigation (for example, a firm 10-15 minutes to check the obvious things -- running processes, recent deployments, resource metrics) before deciding, rather than either escalating instantly with no information or sitting on it indefinitely. Escalating well means bringing a specific, organized status, not just 'I'm stuck' -- what's confirmed so far, what's been ruled out, and the specific help needed -- which reads as competent triage, not as an admission of failure. Continuing to investigate in parallel with the senior person, rather than just handing it off and disengaging, also matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give myself about 10 minutes to check the obvious stuff -- top or htop for what's actually eating CPU, whether anything deployed recently, and the resource metrics in our monitoring dashboard. If I don't have a clear answer by then and it's still actively affecting production, I'd message the on-call senior engineer with exactly what I've checked, what I've ruled out, and what I'm leaning toward, and ask them to jump in rather than disappearing to keep digging alone. I'd remind myself that the decision to escalate isn't about whether it makes me look capable -- it's about how many applications are timing out right now and how long that's already been going on. Bringing a specific status instead of just 'it's broken, help' is what actually makes that escalation read as good triage instead of giving up.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck alone for too long out of fear that escalating looks like failure
Escalating immediately with zero information gathered, forcing the senior person to start from scratch
Escalating vaguely ('it's broken, help') instead of with a specific status and ask
Disengaging entirely after escalating instead of continuing to help in parallel
keyPoints: Decide to escalate based on business impact and time elapsed, not fear of looking incompetent
Time-box the initial solo investigation rather than going indefinitely or escalating instantly
Escalate with a specific status -- confirmed, ruled out, and the specific ask -- not just 'I'm stuck'
Stay engaged and helping after escalating, don't just hand off and disappear

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the escalation decision around impact/time, not ego
Describes a reasonable time-boxed investigation approach
Describes escalating with a specific, organized status

questions.title: Communicating a CI failure that will delay a release
questions.prompt: You're about to merge a pull request for a feature that was supposed to ship today, and the CI pipeline's automated tests fail on a part of the code you didn't even touch. How do you handle this, and what would you communicate to your team about the delay?
questions.modelAnswer: This tests judgment about release discipline and honest communication under time pressure, not raw debugging speed. The core principle is that a failing CI check exists specifically to prevent exactly this situation -- merging and releasing something that doesn't actually pass automated verification -- so the pressure of 'it was supposed to ship today' is not a legitimate reason to merge around a red check or disable the failing test to get past it; doing that defeats the entire purpose of having CI in the first place and risks shipping a real regression. The right first step is investigating whether the failure is genuinely related to a change already merged by someone else (a real regression that needs fixing before anyone ships) or an unrelated flaky/environmental test issue, and communicating that status honestly and promptly to the team rather than either staying silent or quietly forcing the merge through. A strong answer treats the deadline as a factor to communicate about honestly, not a reason to compromise what CI is there to protect.
questions.professionalAnswer: I would not merge through a failing check just because of the deadline pressure -- that's exactly the scenario CI exists to catch, and bypassing it to hit today's date risks shipping something actually broken instead of just shipping something late. My first move is investigating what's actually failing: is this a real regression from something recently merged, or a flaky/environmental test that's unrelated to any real code problem? Either way, I'd message the team right away with the honest status -- CI is currently red on main from an unrelated test, I'm looking into whether it's a real issue or just flaky, and this might push today's release -- rather than staying quiet and hoping it resolves itself or silently merging around it. If it turns out to be a real regression, I'd flag who owns that area and get it fixed before anyone merges anything else on top of a broken main branch. I'd rather communicate a late release honestly than let deadline pressure push a broken CI check through.
commonMistakes: Merging through a failing CI check, or disabling/skipping the failing test, to hit the deadline
Staying silent about the delay instead of communicating the status honestly and promptly
Not distinguishing a genuine regression from an unrelated flaky/environmental test failure before deciding next steps
Treating the deadline as a reason to compromise what CI exists to protect, rather than a factor to communicate about honestly
keyPoints: A failing CI check exists specifically to prevent shipping something broken -- don't merge around it under deadline pressure
Investigate whether the failure is a real regression or an unrelated/flaky test before deciding what to do
Communicate the status honestly and promptly to the team, including the likely impact on the release date
A late, honest release beats an on-time release that bypassed a real failing check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly refuses to merge/bypass a failing CI check for deadline pressure
Describes a sensible investigation approach (regression vs. flaky)
Describes honest, prompt communication of the delay
